plain: A tax move letting an investor sell one Real Estate property and buy another without immediately paying Capital Gain tax — if specific rules are followed.
snappy: Tax-deferred swap of one investment property for another under IRC §1031.
detail: Section 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code defers federal Capital Gain on sale of investment Real Estate if proceeds reinvest into 'like-kind' Real Estate within tight timelines: 45 days to identify replacement property, 180 days to close. A Qualified Intermediary holds proceeds — the investor cannot touch the cash. Primary residences don't qualify; investment property does. Boot (unequal trade value, cash taken out, debt relief) is taxable. The 2017 TCJA restricted 1031 to Real Property only; personal property exchanges no longer qualify.

plain: A condensed legal history of a property — every owner, Lien, and transfer back through time.
snappy: Condensed legal history of a property's ownership and encumbrances.
detail: An abstract is a chronological summary of every recorded document affecting a property's Title — Deeds, Liens, easements, mortgages, court judgments — back to the original land grant or a statutory cut-off. The abstract feeds a title search, which a title company or attorney examines before issuing Title Insurance. In US states where the practice still dominates (the Midwest and parts of the South), the abstract is updated and re-certified at each sale.

plain: A clause that lets the Lender demand the full Mortgage balance immediately if the borrower breaks the loan terms.
snappy: Lender's right to call the entire loan due upon Default.
detail: An acceleration clause is the trigger that turns a missed payment into a Foreclosure. When the borrower breaches the Mortgage (most often by Default on payments), the Lender can declare the full Principal balance due at once instead of just the missed installment. Acceleration is the legal predicate for Foreclosure proceedings in most US states.

plain: The 1990 federal law requiring public accommodations and most commercial properties to be accessible to people with disabilities.
snappy: Federal accessibility law for public accommodations and many commercial properties.
detail: Title III of ADA covers public accommodations and commercial facilities — Retail, Office, restaurants, hotels, healthcare, daycares, and more. New construction and alterations must meet the ADA Standards for Accessible Design (entryways, restrooms, parking, signage, routes). Existing facilities must remove barriers where 'readily achievable.' DOJ enforces; private suits can recover attorney's fees. Multifamily residential under four units is exempt from ADA but covered by the Fair Housing Act's accessibility provisions for first-floor units in buildings of four or more.

plain: A home loan whose interest rate changes on a fixed schedule — cheaper at first than a Fixed-Rate Mortgage, but the payment can rise later.
snappy: Mortgage with an interest rate that resets periodically — lower teaser rate, payment risk later.
detail: An ARM has a fixed introductory rate (commonly 3, 5, 7, or 10 years) followed by periodic adjustments tied to an Index plus a lender Margin. Each reset is bounded by Rate Caps. Conforming ARMs reset to SOFR since the retirement of LIBOR. Borrowers trade lower upfront payments for reset-period risk versus a Fixed-Rate Mortgage.

plain: A small secondary home on the same Lot as a main house — a granny flat, garage conversion, or backyard cottage.
snappy: Secondary independent dwelling on the same Lot as a primary residence.
detail: ADUs include detached cottages, garage conversions, basement apartments, and attached additions with their own kitchen and entrance. Once banned by most US Zoning codes, ADUs were broadly legalised in California (2017+) and Oregon (2017+) as a housing-supply response. ADUs typically share Property Tax with the main parcel but generate rental income or accommodate aging parents. Local rules govern minimum Lot size, parking requirements, and short-term rental restrictions.

plain: A doctrine letting someone who openly occupies another's Land for years eventually claim legal ownership.
snappy: Acquiring Title to Real Property through long, open, hostile possession.
detail: The squatter's law. Requirements vary by state but generally need possession that is open and notorious, continuous, exclusive, hostile (without permission), and lasting for a statutory period (typically 5–20 years). The classic case: a fence built three feet over the property line, undisturbed for the statute. Some states require payment of Property Tax during the period. Once perfected, adverse possession ripens into legal Title and is typically confirmed by a Quiet Title action.

plain: The Fair Housing Act provision requiring HUD funding recipients to actively work to overcome historical patterns of housing discrimination — not just refrain from discriminating.
snappy: Fair Housing Act duty to actively dismantle segregation, not just refrain from discrimination.
detail: AFFH stems from Section 808 of the Fair Housing Act (1968). The 2015 Obama-era AFFH rule required local jurisdictions receiving HUD funds to conduct Assessments of Fair Housing — analysing local segregation, racially concentrated poverty, disparate access to opportunity — and adopt action plans. Trump suspended the rule in 2018, then formally repealed in 2020. Biden 2021 reinstated; the 2023 'AFFH 2.0' rule restored the assessment framework. Politically contentious — alternates with administrations. Localities historically resistant: zoning reforms that AFFH plans recommend conflict with single-family preservation.

plain: A written statement of fact signed under oath — used in real estate to certify identity, marital status, or property condition.
snappy: Sworn written statement of fact, signed and notarised.
detail: Affidavits appear throughout a real estate Closing: the affidavit of Title (seller swears the Title is clean), the survey affidavit (seller swears no boundary changes since the last survey), affidavits of identity, and affidavits of marital status. Each is notarised and recorded. False statements expose the signer to perjury charges. Title Insurance often relies on affidavits to cover risks that aren't visible from public records alone.

plain: Whether a typical household can actually afford homes in a given market — measured against income and Mortgage payment.
snappy: Whether typical households can afford homes in a market.
detail: The NAR Housing Affordability Index measures whether the median-income household can qualify for a Mortgage on the median-priced home. An index of 100 means median household income exactly meets the qualifying income for a 20% Down Payment Mortgage. The 2021-2023 rate spike crashed affordability nationwide — the index fell below 100 for the first time since the 1980s in many metros, locking many would-be buyers out of ownership entirely.

plain: Residential property whose Rent is restricted by Land use covenants, government subsidies, or income limits to remain affordable to lower-income households.
snappy: Residential property with Rent or Sale price restricted to remain affordable to lower-income households.
detail: Affordable housing in the US comes through three main channels. Federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program — most common, subsidises new construction or substantial rehabilitation in exchange for 30+ year affordability covenants. Project-based Section 8 (HUD payments tied to specific buildings). Inclusionary Zoning (developer set-asides at below-market rents in exchange for density bonuses or fee waivers). All three carry deed restrictions or restrictive Covenants that survive ownership changes. Compliance monitoring is intense — annual income certifications, audits, and HUD inspections.

plain: A licensed real estate professional who represents a buyer or seller — paid through Commission at Closing.
snappy: Licensed real estate professional working under a sponsoring Broker.
detail: All US real estate Agents hold a state salesperson licence and operate under a sponsoring Broker. Agents come in two roles in a transaction: the listing Agent represents the seller, the Buyer's Agent represents the buyer. Following the 2024 NAR settlement, buyers and their Agents now sign written representation agreements before tours, with Commission terms negotiated directly. Don't confuse Agent (the licence) with Realtor (NAR membership).

plain: A purchase offer with no Mortgage — the buyer pays the full price from their own funds.
snappy: Purchase offer not contingent on financing — buyer covers the whole price.
detail: All-cash offers carry weight because they remove financing risk: no Appraisal Contingency, no Underwriting delays, no lender pulling out at the eleventh hour. Sellers in competitive markets routinely accept all-cash offers below the highest financed bid. Cash buyers often back into the strategy via investor capital or a later cash-out Refinance.

plain: The way each Mortgage payment chips away at what you owe — early payments mostly cover Interest, later ones mostly cover Principal.
snappy: Schedule that splits each loan payment between Interest and Principal over time.
detail: Amortization is the systematic paydown of a Mortgage's Principal through scheduled payments. In the early years of a 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage, most of each payment covers Interest because the outstanding balance is largest; in the final years, almost all pays down Principal. Lenders provide an amortization schedule at Closing showing the split for every payment.

plain: An independent expert's written estimate of what a property is worth, used by Lenders to decide how much to lend against it.
snappy: Licensed third-party valuation of a property's market value at a point in time.
detail: A residential appraisal is performed by a licensed Appraiser following USPAP methodology and forms the basis for the Lender's LTV calculation. The appraiser inspects the property, pulls Comps, and applies adjustments to estimate market value. A low appraisal can derail a purchase if the Lender refuses to lend against the higher contract price, triggering the Appraisal Contingency.

plain: A clause in a purchase contract letting the buyer back out without penalty if the Appraisal comes in below the contract price.
snappy: Contractual exit if the Appraisal under-values the property.
detail: If the property's Appraised Value lands below the contract price, the Lender will only finance against the lower number — leaving the buyer to cover the gap in cash. The Appraisal Contingency lets the buyer renegotiate or walk and recover the Earnest Money Deposit. A standard residential Contingency, but waivable in competitive markets. Commercial transactions handle this through a broader Due Diligence period rather than a separate contingency.

plain: The dollar number the Appraiser writes in their report — what the property is judged to be worth.
snappy: Stated dollar value from the Appraiser for a property in a written Appraisal report.
detail: Appraised Value anchors the Lender's LTV calculation. When appraised value falls below the contract price, the Lender will only finance against the lower number — the buyer must come up with the gap in cash, renegotiate, or back out via the Appraisal Contingency. Appraised value is distinct from Assessed Value (used for Property Tax) and market value (what buyers will actually pay).

plain: The licensed professional who writes an Appraisal — independent of the buyer, seller, and Lender.
snappy: Licensed third party who values property under USPAP standards.
detail: Appraisers are licensed at the state level under federal Appraiser Qualifications Board minimums. They must follow USPAP and are independent of the parties to a transaction. The 2008 financial crisis tightened appraiser-independence rules: Lenders now order Appraisals through Appraisal Management Companies rather than directly, to prevent pressure on valuations.

plain: The all-in cost of a Mortgage per year, including the interest rate plus Closing Costs and Discount Points.
snappy: True annual cost of a loan including fees, expressed as a percentage.
detail: APR sits next to the headline interest rate on every Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure so borrowers can compare apples to apples. A loan with a low interest rate but high Discount Points and origination fees can have a higher APR than a slightly higher rate with no points. APR assumes the borrower keeps the loan to maturity; in practice most Refinance or move first.

plain: A common shorthand for an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage.
snappy: Standard shorthand for an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage.
detail: ARM is universal shorthand in US mortgage lending for an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage. Naming follows a fixed/variable convention: a 5/1 ARM has a 5-year fixed period then annual resets; a 7/6 ARM has 7 years fixed then 6-month resets. Use the full term name in the first mention of a definition, then ARM thereafter — the reader knows the shorthand. See Adjustable-Rate Mortgage for full mechanics.

plain: A safety limit on how much the interest rate on an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage can rise — both at each adjustment and over the loan's life.
snappy: Rate ceiling on an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage, per-period and lifetime.
detail: ARM Caps protect borrowers from runaway resets. A typical 5/1 ARM has caps written as 2/2/5: 2% maximum first adjustment, 2% maximum per subsequent adjustment, 5% maximum over the loan's life. Without caps, a sudden Index spike (the 2022 Fed hiking cycle is the canonical example) could double a borrower's payment overnight. Caps are disclosed on the Loan Estimate.

plain: A sale between two unrelated parties acting in their own interests — the standard assumption for market value.
snappy: Sale between unrelated parties, each acting in their own interest.
detail: Arm's length is the assumption underlying market-value Appraisal and Comp selection. Sales between family members, between an entity and its principals, or under coercion (Foreclosure, short sale, distress) are not arm's length and don't establish market value cleanly. Lenders and Appraisers scrutinise non-arm's-length transactions: the IRS may treat below-market family sales as gifts, and the Lender may underwrite differently when buyer and seller share interests.

plain: An investor's estimate of what a fixer-upper will be worth after renovation, used to size the purchase budget.
snappy: Projected market value after planned renovations are complete.
detail: ARV is the cornerstone metric in fix-and-flip and BRRRR (buy-rehab-rent-refinance-repeat) strategies. Investors back into a maximum purchase price by subtracting renovation costs and target profit from ARV. Hard-money Lenders typically cap loans at 70-75% of ARV. The Appraisal of an as-is distressed property is usually well below ARV — that's the spread the investor monetises.

plain: The dollar value a county assessor assigns to your property to calculate Property Tax — usually below market value.
snappy: County assessor's value used to compute Property Tax.
detail: Assessed Value is the figure local tax authorities assign for Property Tax purposes. It is typically a percentage of fair market value (the assessment ratio) and updates on a reassessment cycle that varies by jurisdiction — annually in some counties, every 3-5 years in others. Distinct from Appraised Value (a Lender's number, set by a licensed Appraiser) and from sale price (what a buyer actually pays).

plain: A Mortgage the buyer can take over from the seller at the seller's existing interest rate — valuable when rates have risen since.
snappy: Mortgage that can be transferred from seller to buyer at the existing rate.
detail: VA Loans and FHA Loans are typically assumable; conventional Conforming Loans usually are not. Assumption became newly valuable after the 2022 rate spike: a buyer assuming a 3% Mortgage saved hundreds per month versus a fresh 7% loan. The new buyer must qualify with the Lender, and the seller often remains contingently liable unless formally released.

plain: A second-place purchase offer that activates if the first deal falls through.
snappy: Second-position offer that takes effect if the primary contract dies.
detail: When a seller has multiple offers and accepts one, runners-up can sign a backup-offer contract that becomes binding automatically if the primary deal terminates within a stated window. Backup buyers usually post smaller Earnest Money since their offer may never activate. Sellers value strong backup offers because they discipline the primary buyer's behaviour — knowing a backup is waiting reduces the buyer's leverage in inspection renegotiations.

plain: A Mortgage with low monthly payments — often Interest-Only — but a large lump-sum Balloon Payment due at the end of a short term, usually 5-7 years.
snappy: Mortgage with low recurring payments and a large lump-sum due at term end.
detail: Balloon Mortgages persist in Commercial Real Estate (typical 5-10 year balloon on a 25-30 year amortising schedule) and in small-Lender residential portfolios. The borrower pays as if Amortizing over 30 years but owes the remaining Principal at the balloon date — refinance, sale, or restructure required at maturity. Post-Dodd-Frank, residential balloon Mortgages are restricted: small Lenders can originate Qualified Mortgage Balloons in rural areas, otherwise prohibited. Commercial balloons are unrestricted, and the maturity walls of CMBS pools concentrate enormous refinance risk into specific months.

plain: A big lump-sum payment due at the end of a loan that wasn't fully amortised over its term.
snappy: Final lump-sum payment that pays off the remaining loan balance.
detail: Balloon loans have low monthly payments because they amortise as if the loan ran longer than its actual term — e.g., 30-year Amortization but a 7-year term with the full remaining Principal due as a balloon. Common in commercial Mortgages and Bridge Loans. Residential borrowers often refinance before the balloon hits, so a Refinance market shock can leave a borrower trapped.

plain: A Deed conveying property with implied (but not explicit) ownership warranty — the grantor implies they own the property but warrants nothing further.
snappy: Deed conveying property with implied ownership warranty but no further warranties.
detail: Bargain and Sale Deed sits between Warranty Deed (strong warranties) and Quitclaim Deed (no warranties). The implied covenant: the grantor implies ownership of the property they're conveying. Beyond that, no covenant against Encumbrances, no warranty of Title, no defense obligation. Common in tax sales, fiduciary sales (executor, trustee), and foreclosure sales — situations where the grantor cannot or will not warrant. New York, Vermont, and some other Eastern states use Bargain and Sale Deeds with or without covenants as a routine conveyance form. Title Insurance fills the warranty gap for the buyer.

plain: The fixed Rent in a Commercial Lease, before any pass-through Operating Expenses, percentage Rent, or Escalations — the headline number quoted PSF.
snappy: Fixed Rent before Operating Expense pass-throughs or percentage components.
detail: Base Rent is the starting line. Commercial Real Estate quotes Base Rent in dollars per rentable square foot per year ($/RSF/year). On top sit: Triple Net pass-throughs (Property Tax, insurance, CAM in NNN structures), Escalation Clauses (annual bumps), percentage Rent (Retail only, above sales thresholds), and ancillary income. The full effective Rent the Tenant pays often runs 20-50% above Base Rent depending on Lease structure. Multifamily and Residential Leases typically quote 'Rent' as a single all-in number rather than splitting Base Rent and pass-throughs.

plain: One one-hundredth of a percent — the standard unit for talking about interest rate moves.
snappy: 1/100 of one percent — the language of rate changes.
detail: A basis point — abbreviated bps and pronounced bips — is 0.01%. A Mortgage Rate moving from 6.50% to 6.75% rose 25 basis points. Used wherever small percentage differences matter: pricing the Margin on an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage, comparing Cap Rate compression between markets, or quoting Spread above a benchmark.

plain: The Lender named in a Deed of Trust — the party entitled to be paid back, with the right to direct the Trustee to Foreclose on Default.
snappy: The Lender in a Deed of Trust — entitled to repayment and Foreclosure-direction rights.
detail: In a Deed of Trust, the Beneficiary is the Lender — the party entitled to repayment of the Mortgage. When the borrower pays in full, the Beneficiary directs the Trustee to record a reconveyance, clearing Title. When the borrower defaults, the Beneficiary directs the Trustee to commence non-judicial Foreclosure under the power-of-sale clause. Loan servicing rights can be sold; the new servicer becomes Beneficiary of record. In estate-planning Trusts and Title Insurance escrow trusts, 'beneficiary' refers to the person entitled to receive trust assets — same word, different mechanism.

plain: The illegal practice of frightening homeowners into selling cheap by claiming minorities are moving in, then reselling at higher prices to incoming buyers — a Fair Housing Act violation.
snappy: Illegal Fair Housing Act practice of inducing panic sales through race-based scare tactics.
detail: Blockbusting was a structural tactic in mid-20th-century US neighbourhood turnover. Real Estate operators would buy one home in a white neighbourhood, list it to a Black family, then canvass remaining white homeowners with predictions of plummeting values, urging quick sales at below-market prices. The operator then resold at substantially higher prices to incoming Black buyers — turning neighbourhoods over within years. Banned under the Fair Housing Act since 1968. Still surfaces in subtler forms: agent solicitation flyers in 'changing' neighbourhoods, deceptive market characterisations, predatory cash-buyer outreach.

plain: A federal tax break that lets owners write off a big chunk of certain Real Estate improvements in the first year, instead of spreading over decades.
snappy: First-year accelerated write-off of qualified property and certain improvements.
detail: Bonus Depreciation under IRC §168(k) sat at 100% from 2017 (TCJA) through 2022 — Cost Segregation studies surged in popularity to maximise first-year deductions. Phasedown: 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 20% in 2026, 0% in 2027 absent congressional action. Applies to property with 20-year-or-less recovery period — typically 5, 7, and 15-year personal-property components inside a building (carpeting, cabinets, parking lots, landscaping) identified through Cost Segregation. Real Property (39-year commercial, 27.5-year residential rental) doesn't qualify directly.

plain: Any value received in a 1031 Exchange that isn't like-kind Real Property — cash, debt relief, or personal property — taxed as Capital Gain.
snappy: Non-like-kind value received in a 1031 Exchange — cash, debt relief, personal property.
detail: Boot taints the tax-deferred nature of a 1031 Exchange to the extent of the boot amount. Two common boot types. (1) Cash boot: investor receives cash from the Qualified Intermediary at the end of the Exchange. (2) Mortgage boot: replacement property has a smaller Mortgage than the relinquished property, so debt relief is treated as boot. Boot is taxed first as Depreciation Recapture (ordinary rates capped at 25% for §1250), then as Capital Gain. Strategies to avoid: trade up in both Sale Price and debt, or use exchange-only proceeds with no cash sweep.

plain: A quick estimate by a real estate Broker of what a home is worth, cheaper and faster than a full Appraisal.
snappy: Licensed broker's informal valuation — quicker than a formal Appraisal.
detail: A Broker Price Opinion is a written estimate of likely sale price prepared by a licensed real estate Broker. BPOs are used by Lenders and servicers for portfolio decisions — short sales, REO disposition, and Refinance — where a full Appraisal compliant with USPAP is not required by regulation. BPOs cost a fraction of an Appraisal but carry less legal weight and cannot be used to set LTV at origination.

plain: Short-term financing that lets a buyer purchase a new home before selling their current one.
snappy: Short-term Mortgage that bridges the gap between two transactions.
detail: Bridge Loans are 6-12 month loans secured against the borrower's existing home (or both homes) so they can put a non-contingent offer on the next property before selling the first. Higher interest rate than a standard Mortgage and often structured with a Balloon Payment at term end. Commercial real estate uses bridge loans for acquisition or repositioning before securing permanent financing.

plain: A licensed real estate professional who can run their own brokerage and supervise agents.
snappy: Licensed real estate professional senior to an agent; can run a brokerage.
detail: All US states distinguish between a salesperson licence (often called an agent) and a broker licence. Brokers complete more coursework and exam content, can operate independently, sponsor agent licences, hold escrow funds, and sign as Broker of Record on transactions. A Buyer's Agent and a listing agent typically work under a sponsoring Broker who shares the commission.

plain: A real-estate investor strategy: buy cheap, fix up, rent out, Refinance to pull cash back out, and repeat with the next property.
snappy: Investor strategy of buying distressed property, rehabbing, renting, refinancing equity out, repeating.
detail: BRRRR popularised through investor podcasts and forums (BiggerPockets) as a way to scale a rental portfolio with limited starting capital. Mechanics: buy below market (often distressed or auction), spend on Rehab to lift ARV, place a Tenant to stabilise income, Refinance against the new value to recapture invested cash, recycle into the next deal. Risks: Appraisal coming in low at refi, rate environment changes during seasoning, Tenant placement delays. Hard Money often funds the buy-and-rehab phase.

plain: A development strategy of building Single-Family or townhome subdivisions specifically as Rental property — not for sale to homeowners — managed institutionally like Multifamily.
snappy: Development of Single-Family or townhome subdivisions purpose-built as Rental property.
detail: Build-to-Rent emerged as a distinct asset class in the 2010s and accelerated in the 2020s. Operators (American Homes 4 Rent, Tricon, NexMetro, Pretium, Invitation Homes' BTR programs) develop entire neighbourhoods of 100-300 detached homes or townhomes designed for rental from day one — communal amenities (pool, fitness, dog park), centralised maintenance, smart-home packages, professional Property Manager. Target Tenants: families priced out of Single-Family home purchase who want yard and house but won't bid against owner-occupier buyers. Strong post-2020 demographic tailwind; Cap Rate spread to traditional Multifamily compresses as the asset class matures.

plain: Local rules setting minimum construction standards — structural, fire, electrical, plumbing.
snappy: Local minimum-standards rules for building construction and renovation.
detail: Building Codes are adopted by states and modified by local jurisdictions to govern construction safety, materials, and energy efficiency. The International Code Council's I-Codes are the most widely adopted base. Permits are required for work that affects code-regulated systems; inspections verify compliance at each stage. Construction outside Building Code creates liability for the owner at resale and may prevent issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy.

plain: Local-government authorisation to build, remodel, or demolish — required for most structural work.
snappy: Government approval required before construction work begins.
detail: Building Permits force construction to comply with Building Code via inspection at each stage (foundation, framing, mechanical, final). Unpermitted work creates resale problems: buyers' lenders may refuse to finance, Insurers may deny claims, and the local authority can force retroactive permitting or demolition. Unpermitted square footage typically gets excluded from Appraised Value. Most jurisdictions require permits for additions, structural changes, electrical and plumbing work, and pool installation.

plain: Paying upfront fees to permanently or temporarily reduce a Mortgage's interest rate.
snappy: Upfront cash to lower a Mortgage rate, permanent or for the first few years.
detail: A permanent buy-down works through Discount Points — each point typically lowers the rate ~0.25%. Temporary buy-downs (2-1 or 3-2-1) lower the rate for the first 2-3 years, then step back to the note rate. Builders and sellers often fund buy-downs as a buyer incentive when high interest rates suppress demand — concealing what amounts to a price cut as a financing perk.

plain: The person or entity acquiring a property — represented in the transaction by a Buyer's Agent.
snappy: Party acquiring the property in a real estate transaction.
detail: The Buyer is the party purchasing the property — an individual, a couple, an LLC, a Trust, or a corporation. In most US residential transactions the Buyer works through a Buyer's Agent under a Buyer Representation Agreement. The Buyer makes the offer, signs the Mortgage, pays Closing Costs, takes Title at Closing, and assumes Property Tax and insurance from that date forward.

plain: A written contract between a buyer and a Buyer's Agent setting out the agent's duties and the buyer's Commission obligations.
snappy: Written contract defining a Buyer's Agent's duties and Commission terms.
detail: Buyer Representation Agreements became mandatory before MLS access in late 2024 following the NAR settlement. The agreement specifies: how long the relationship runs, the geographic and property scope, the Buyer's Agent's fiduciary duties, and exactly what Commission the buyer agrees to pay (cash or seller-funded) on a successful purchase. Before the settlement, buy-side Commission was implicit in the MLS listing; now it's a direct negotiation.

plain: The real estate agent who works for you when you're buying — they hunt for properties and negotiate on your side.
snappy: Real estate agent representing the buyer in a transaction.
detail: A buyer's agent has a fiduciary duty to the buyer — confidentiality, loyalty, disclosure — and is typically paid via Commission split with the listing agent at Closing. Following the 2024 NAR settlement, buyers and their agents now sign written representation agreements before tours, with Commission terms negotiated directly rather than implied through the MLS listing. A Buyer's Agent works under a sponsoring Broker.

plain: The operational rulebook of an HOA or Condo — how boards are elected, how meetings are held, how budgets are approved, how Special Assessments get levied.
snappy: Operational rulebook of an HOA or Condo — board elections, meetings, budgets, assessments.
detail: Bylaws sit alongside the Condo Declaration and CC&Rs in the HOA/Condo governing-document hierarchy. The Declaration creates the entity and defines property; CC&Rs govern owner behaviour; bylaws govern association operations. Typical bylaw provisions: board size and composition, election timing and procedures, officer roles, quorum requirements, voting procedures (in-person, mail, electronic), committee structures, annual meeting protocols, budget approval thresholds, Special Assessment procedures. Bylaws can be amended without amending the Declaration — easier process — and are the most actively updated of the three.

plain: Shorthand for Common Area Maintenance — the operating costs Landlords incur for shared spaces (parking, lobbies, landscaping) that get charged back to Commercial Tenants.
snappy: Common Area Maintenance — operating costs for shared spaces charged back to Tenants.
detail: CAM charges cover the recurring cost of keeping common spaces functional and presentable: parking lot maintenance, snow removal, landscaping, common-area lighting, signage, security, janitorial. Allocation: pro-rata by leased square footage. NNN Leases pass CAM straight through; Modified Gross caps at base year amounts; Gross Leases absorb into Base Rent. CAM Reconciliation annually trues up actual CAM expense against estimated CAM billed during the year. Tenant audit rights and CAM caps are heavily negotiated. Property Manager budgeting accuracy matters — surprises hurt Tenant relationships and trigger audits.

plain: A quick yardstick for what an investment property earns each year, expressed as a percentage of what it costs.
snappy: Annual NOI divided by purchase price — back-of-envelope yield on a commercial property.
detail: Cap Rate equals Net Operating Income divided by property value. A 5% cap means $50,000 of NOI on a $1M property. Higher cap rates signal higher perceived risk or weaker markets; lower caps signal premium assets in strong markets. Cap rates ignore financing, taxes, and capex — useful for comparing deals quickly, dangerous as a sole metric. The reciprocal of cap rate is the price-to-NOI multiple.

plain: When investor capital flooding into Real Estate pushes purchase prices up faster than NOI grows — Cap Rates fall, meaning lower yield per dollar invested.
snappy: Falling Cap Rates driven by investor demand outpacing NOI growth — yields compress.
detail: Cap Rate compression dominated 2015-2022 Commercial Real Estate. Institutional capital chasing yield in a low-interest-rate environment pushed Multifamily Going-In Cap Rates from 6% to 4% in many markets — meaning a property generating $1M of NOI sold for $25M instead of $16.7M. Aggressive Sponsor pro formas extrapolated continued compression into Exit Cap Rate assumptions; when rates spiked in 2022, compression reversed and Exit Caps widened by 100-200 basis points, gutting projected IRR on deals underwritten at peak.

plain: Big spending on a property that improves or replaces a long-lived asset — roof, HVAC, parking lot — rather than routine repair.
snappy: Major property spending on improvements or long-lived assets, distinct from Operating Expenses.
detail: The Cap-Ex line sits below NOI in the cash flow waterfall. Distinguishing Cap-Ex from Operating Expenses changes both tax treatment (depreciated over years vs. expensed immediately) and reported NOI. IRS rules under Sections 162 and 263 govern the line. Industry shorthand: roof replacement, HVAC, parking lot resurfacing, elevator modernisation, façade work all sit in Cap-Ex. Filter replacement, janitorial, painting, minor repairs sit in Operating Expenses. Pro forma builds a Replacement Reserve to fund predictable Cap-Ex cycles.

plain: The full spelling of Cap-Ex — big spending on a property that improves or replaces a long-lived asset.
snappy: Full spelling of Cap-Ex — major spending on improvements or long-lived property assets.
detail: Capital Expenditure is the formal accounting term that Cap-Ex shortens. IRS rules under Sections 162 and 263 govern whether spending is capitalised (depreciated over years) or expensed immediately. The line between Capital Expenditure and Operating Expenses changes both tax treatment and reported NOI. See Cap-Ex for the practical roster of which property items qualify and how Replacement Reserves fund them in stabilised property.

plain: The profit when you sell a property for more than what you paid plus improvements — taxed at federal long-term rates after one year.
snappy: Profit on sale of property; long-term rates apply after one year held.
detail: Capital gain equals sale price minus selling costs minus cost basis (purchase price plus capitalised improvements). Held over a year, long-term capital-gains rates apply (0%, 15%, or 20% federal depending on income, plus state). The Section 121 primary-residence exclusion shelters up to $250K of gain ($500K married) for owners who lived in the property 2 of the past 5 years. Investment property uses a 1031 Exchange to defer gain into the next property.

plain: The layered structure of all the money funding a Real Estate deal — senior debt at the bottom, equity at the top, with mezzanine and preferred equity sometimes filling in between.
snappy: Layered structure of all debt and equity funding a Real Estate deal.
detail: From safest to riskiest: Senior debt (50-65% of project cost, lowest rate, first claim on cash and collateral) → Mezzanine debt (5-15%, higher rate, secured by entity rather than property) → Preferred Equity (5-15%, fixed return ahead of common equity) → Common Equity (the Sponsor and LP capital, residual claim). Each layer prices according to its risk position. Restructuring during distress works down the stack — lender forbearance, mezz capitalisation, equity wipe-out. Sophisticated capital-stack design is the heart of institutional Real Estate finance.

plain: The cross-industry term for what Real Estate calls Promote — the Sponsor's share of profits above an investor return hurdle, taxed at lower long-term Capital Gain rates.
snappy: Sponsor's share of profits above hurdles, taxed at long-term Capital Gain rates.
detail: Carried interest is the private-equity term that subsumes Real Estate's Promote, hedge-fund 20%, and venture-capital carry. Federal tax treats carry on holdings of three or more years as long-term Capital Gain — taxed at 20% rather than the 37% top ordinary rate. Many proposals to tax carry as ordinary income have failed (2016, 2017, 2021, 2022 negotiations). The TCJA tightened the rule by extending the holding-period threshold from 1 year to 3 years. Real Estate's typical 5-7 year Hold Period comfortably meets the 3-year bar.

plain: The monthly bills of owning a property — Mortgage, Property Tax, insurance, utilities, upkeep.
snappy: Ongoing monthly costs of holding a property.
detail: Carrying costs include the Mortgage payment (Principal plus Interest), Property Tax, homeowners insurance, utilities, HOA dues if applicable, and routine maintenance. For investors, carrying costs are the burn during vacancy or rehab — the gap between purchase and rent commencement that has to be funded out of pocket. Cash-on-Cash Return is computed net of carrying costs.

plain: Annual cash flow from a property divided by the cash you put in — your money's actual yield.
snappy: Annual pre-tax cash flow divided by initial cash invested.
detail: Cash-on-Cash Return measures the yield on the equity actually invested, not the property's total value — so it captures the leverage effect of a Mortgage. A property with a 5% Cap Rate financed at 75% LTV can produce 10%+ cash-on-cash when rents cover the debt service. Used alongside Cap Rate and IRR to evaluate income properties; favoured for its simplicity.

plain: A Refinance where the borrower replaces an existing Mortgage with a larger one — taking the difference in cash.
snappy: Refinance into a larger Mortgage with the borrower taking the difference in cash.
detail: Cash-out refis let homeowners tap built-up Equity without selling. Typical use: home improvements, debt consolidation, education, business capital, investment property purchase. Lender restrictions on combined-LTV: typically 80% for Conventional Loans, 80% for FHA Loans, 90% for VA Loans (effectively up to 100%). Higher rate than rate-term Refinance (50-75 basis points). Loan officers must disclose if the new payment exceeds the prior one. Interest deductibility under TCJA: only deductible if used for substantial home improvements, not for personal expenses.

plain: The rule book of a HOA or planned community — covers what owners can do with their property and what they pay.
snappy: Recorded private rules binding every owner in a HOA community.
detail: CC&Rs are recorded with the county and run with the land — every successor owner is bound. They typically govern paint colours, fencing, parking, pet limits, short-term-rental rules, and HOA dues. CC&Rs sit alongside the HOA bylaws (governance rules) and articles (entity formation). Buyers should review CC&Rs during Due Diligence — restrictions on use, satellite dishes, or rentals can be deal-breakers. Some old CC&Rs contain unenforceable discriminatory language that survives on paper but cannot be enforced.

plain: The official local-government sign-off that a building is safe to live in — required before owners can move in.
snappy: Local sign-off declaring a building safe and legal to occupy.
detail: A CO is issued by the local building department after all required inspections pass — typically structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and final. New construction cannot legally be occupied without one. Renovations that change the use class (converting commercial to residential) usually require a new CO. Title companies often condition Closing on the CO's issuance for new builds. Some older properties operate under grandfathered occupancy without a modern CO.

plain: The federal agency that regulates consumer mortgages and writes the rules Lenders must follow when lending to homebuyers.
snappy: US federal consumer-finance regulator overseeing Mortgages.
detail: The CFPB was created in 2010 under the Dodd-Frank Act in response to the 2008 financial crisis. It enforces consumer-finance laws including TILA and RESPA, wrote the TRID disclosure rule, and supervises non-bank Mortgage Lenders. Its complaints database and enforcement actions discipline Lenders for unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices. Borrowers can file complaints directly with the CFPB if a Lender mishandles their loan.

plain: The full historical sequence of Deed transfers showing how the Title moved from owner to owner.
snappy: Sequence of recorded Deeds linking current owner back through prior owners.
detail: An unbroken chain of Title — each owner properly conveying via recorded Deed to the next — is what Title Insurance verifies before issuing a policy. A break (a missing recorded transfer, an unprobated will, a forged Deed) creates a cloud on Title that must be cured by quiet-title action, affidavit, or curative document. Chain-of-Title problems are the single most common source of Title Insurance claims.

plain: A state-created insurance company providing Homeowners Insurance in markets where private insurers won't write — Florida's is the largest, covering hurricane and flood risk many private carriers exit.
snappy: State-run insurer of last resort for properties private carriers won't cover.
detail: Florida's Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, created in 2002, is the prototype. It writes Homeowners Insurance in coastal and high-risk areas where private carriers withdraw — and has grown to roughly 1.4 million policies (2024) amid hurricane-driven private-market collapse. California FAIR Plan is the wildfire equivalent (~250,000 policies, growing). Louisiana Citizens, Texas Windstorm Insurance Association similar. Premiums are state-set, often below true risk-adjusted price; deficits trigger assessments on all in-state property-insurance policyholders. Insurance of last resort by design — broader, deeper, costlier coverage than private market.

plain: The highest grade of commercial property — newest, best-located, premium finishes, top rents and lowest vacancy.
snappy: Top grade of commercial property — newest, best-located, premium rents.
detail: Class A property anchors institutional portfolios. Defined relative to local market: a Class A building in suburban Phoenix differs from a Class A in midtown Manhattan. Common attributes: built or substantially renovated in the last 15-20 years, prime location with strong access, full amenity package, blue-chip tenant roster, premium asking Rent (top quartile of submarket). Class A trades at the tightest Cap Rates because risk is lowest. Pension funds, sovereign wealth, and listed REITs concentrate here.

plain: The middle grade of commercial property — older but well-maintained, decent locations, market-average rents.
snappy: Middle grade of commercial property — older, well-kept, market-rate Rents.
detail: Class B is where most US Commercial Real Estate sits. Buildings 20-40 years old, dated finishes, functional but unspectacular. Cap Rates trade 75-150 basis points wider than Class A for the same submarket. Value-add Sponsors target Class B for renovation to lift NOI toward Class A pricing — light Rehab on common areas, unit interiors, mechanical systems. Class B office took the biggest 2020-2023 occupancy hit as Class A absorbed flight-to-quality demand.

plain: The lower grade of commercial property — older, deferred maintenance, secondary locations, below-market Rents.
snappy: Lower grade of commercial property — older, sometimes deferred-maintenance, below-market rents.
detail: Class C property earns the widest Cap Rates and the highest yield-on-cost — at the cost of higher Tenant turnover, more management intensity, and meaningful Cap-Ex needs. Often 40+ years old with deferred maintenance, functional obsolescence, and locations away from prime corridors. Workforce-housing Multifamily and value-add Class C office are common Sponsor strategies. Class C suffers most in down cycles and recovers slowest in up cycles. Lender appetite is thinner — bridge debt and Hard Money fill more of the capital stack.

plain: The final step of a property sale where the Deed transfers and money changes hands.
snappy: Settlement meeting where ownership transfers and funds settle.
detail: At Closing the seller signs the Deed, the buyer signs the Mortgage and note, Escrow releases funds, Title Insurance attaches, and the Deed is recorded with the county. Closing also marks settlement of Closing Costs, prorated Property Tax, and remaining Earnest Money Deposit credits. Increasingly handled remotely with e-signatures and remote online notarisation. Also called settlement or completion depending on the region.

plain: All the fees you pay at the finish line of a home purchase — usually 2-5% of the price on top of the Down Payment.
snappy: Bundle of fees and prepaid items paid at Closing, separate from purchase price.
detail: Closing costs include Lender fees (origination, Underwriting, Appraisal), third-party fees (Title Insurance, Escrow, recording), prepaid items (Property Tax, insurance, Mortgage Interest), and government taxes. Buyers pay 2-5% of price in most US markets. The Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure (TRID forms) itemise every charge. Sellers can be asked to cover some closing costs as a negotiation concession.

plain: The final paperwork the Lender must give you three days before Closing, listing every cost and term.
snappy: required by TRID form detailing final loan terms and Closing Costs.
detail: The Closing Disclosure replaced the HUD-1 Settlement Statement under TRID rules in 2015. Lenders must deliver it at least three business days before Closing so borrowers have time to verify costs against the earlier Loan Estimate. Material changes (different APR, different loan product, prepayment penalty added) reset the three-day clock. The form covers interest rate, monthly payment, every Closing Cost line item, and cash-to-close.

plain: A pending claim or defect that makes Title less than marketable — anything from an unreleased Lien to a heir contesting Probate to a forged Deed in the chain.
snappy: Pending claim or defect that makes Title less than marketable.
detail: Clouds on title surface in title searches: unreleased Mortgages from prior owners, Liens that never got removed, deceased owners whose interest never transferred, forgeries, Adverse Possession claims, missing signatures on historical Deeds, recordings under wrong legal description. Curing a cloud might mean: tracking down a prior owner for a release, filing Quitclaim Deeds from heirs, court-ordered Quiet Title actions, statutory cure proceedings. Title Insurance covers some clouds the title search missed; uncured clouds disclosed at Closing typically delay or kill the transaction.

plain: Bonds backed by pools of Commercial Real Estate mortgages — investors get paid from the rent and Principal of the underlying buildings.
snappy: Bonds backed by pools of Commercial Real Estate mortgages.
detail: CMBS bundle Commercial Mortgages on office, retail, industrial, hotel, and Multifamily property into tranched securities sold to institutional investors. Senior tranches (AAA) absorb losses last; junior tranches (BB and below) absorb first. Loans inside CMBS are typically 10-year, fixed-rate, non-recourse, with strict prepayment penalties (defeasance or yield maintenance). Issuance peaked pre-2008, collapsed, recovered, and softened again post-2020 as office vacancies stressed legacy pools. Special servicers handle workouts when borrowers default.

plain: A building where owners hold shares in a corporation that owns the whole building, rather than owning their unit individually.
snappy: Building owned by a corporation; residents own shares plus a proprietary lease.
detail: Distinct from a Condo: a co-op shareholder doesn't own real estate at all — they own shares in the corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease to a specific apartment. Co-op boards screen buyers, often rejecting applicants for opaque reasons. Financing is harder (many Lenders don't lend on co-ops; share loans replace Mortgages). Common in NYC where ~75% of pre-war buildings are co-ops; rare elsewhere.

plain: The process of turning a rental Multifamily building in NYC and other co-op-heavy markets into a cooperative corporation with shareholder-owners — historically dominant pre-1990s.
snappy: Process converting a rental Multifamily into a cooperative corporation with shareholder-owners.
detail: Co-op conversion was the dominant urban Multifamily-to-ownership conversion in NYC and a few other markets through the 1970s-1990s. Two flavours: eviction-plan conversion (Tenants forced to buy or vacate — used widely 1979-1985 then largely banned in NYC) and non-eviction-plan conversion (Tenants get insider price and right to stay as renters, but can buy at retail). NYC Martin Act regulates conversion offerings, requiring detailed offering plans approved by the AG. The shift from Condo Conversion in newer markets reflects co-op's specific NYC dominance; Condo is the national default elsewhere.

plain: Income-producing real estate — offices, retail, industrial, hotels, multifamily — bought to generate rent rather than to live in.
snappy: Income-producing real estate held as investment rather than primary residence.
detail: Commercial Real Estate spans office, retail, industrial, multifamily (5+ units), hospitality, and specialty segments — anything held for rental income or investment return. CRE financing, valuation (Cap Rate, NOI, DSCR), Underwriting standards, and Leasing structures differ materially from residential. Owners are typically LLCs or partnerships rather than individuals; transactions involve longer Due Diligence and more sophisticated counsel.

plain: The percentage of the sale price paid to real estate agents at Closing — historically 5-6% split between buyer and listing sides.
snappy: Percentage of sale price paid to real estate agents at Closing.
detail: Real estate Commission is paid by the seller out of sale proceeds, traditionally 5-6% split between the listing agent and the Buyer's Agent. The 2024 NAR settlement decoupled Commission from the MLS — buyers and their agents now sign written representation agreements with explicit Commission terms before tours, and the listing no longer advertises a buy-side Commission. Effects on average Commission rates are still settling out as of 2026.

plain: Parts of a Condo or planned community that everyone owns and shares — lobbies, pools, roofs, hallways.
snappy: Shared portions of a Condo or planned community.
detail: Common Areas in a Condo include hallways, lobbies, elevators, the roof, exterior walls, mechanical rooms, and amenities. Each unit owner holds an undivided fractional interest in the Common Area alongside fee-simple ownership of their unit. The HOA maintains Common Areas and funds them via owner dues. Limited Common Areas (a balcony, parking space, storage unit) are common areas assigned to one unit's exclusive use.

plain: In nine states, anything either spouse earns or buys during marriage is owned 50/50 — separately tracked from pre-marital or inherited property.
snappy: Marital-property regime in nine states treating earnings during marriage as 50/50 owned.
detail: Community Property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, Wisconsin. (Alaska, Tennessee, and a few others permit opt-in.) Anything acquired during marriage is community property regardless of titling; pre-marital property and inheritances remain separate. At death of one spouse, the survivor receives a full step-up in basis on the entire community-property home (versus 50% step-up in common-law states) — a major federal income-tax advantage. Divorce courts split community property equally.

plain: A recently sold home similar to yours, used as evidence of what your home is worth.
snappy: Recently sold property similar in size, location, and features — anchors a valuation.
detail: Comps are the working currency of real estate valuation. Appraisers, agents, and investors pull three to six recently closed sales of similar properties within roughly a mile and adjust for differences in square footage, lot, bedrooms, condition, and view to estimate subject value. The sales comparison approach dominates residential Appraisal; commercial Appraisal uses income and cost approaches alongside it.

plain: Free or discounted Rent and other incentives Landlords offer to attract Tenants — months free, reduced Security Deposit, gift cards, TI allowances above market.
snappy: Discounts or freebies Landlords offer to attract Tenants — months free, reduced deposit, TI bumps.
detail: Concessions surge in soft Lease-up markets and disappear in tight ones. Multifamily: 1-2 months free on a 12-month Lease is a typical recession-era concession (effectively 8-17% Rent discount net of the free months). Office and Retail: above-market Tenant Improvement allowances, free Rent periods of 6-12+ months on long Leases. Economic occupancy distinguishes properties running market-rate Rent from those papering over with concessions — physical occupancy can be 95% while effective occupancy is 80%. Underwriting models 'effective Rent' net of concessions, not 'face Rent'.

plain: A Zoning approval for a use not allowed by right, but allowed if specific conditions are met — like a daycare in a residential zone.
snappy: Zoning approval for a use allowed only under specified conditions.
detail: Conditional uses are listed in the Zoning ordinance — they're permitted as of right only if the applicant can demonstrate compatibility with the neighbourhood and meet specific conditions (hours of operation, traffic mitigation, buffer landscaping, parking minimums). The local planning commission or board reviews; some jurisdictions require city council approval. Common conditional uses: schools, churches, daycares, group homes, gas stations, drive-throughs, cell towers. Granted CUPs run with the Land but can be revoked if conditions are violated.

plain: An individually owned unit inside a larger building where common areas are shared and run by an HOA.
snappy: Individually owned unit (own Deed) with shared common areas and HOA governance.
detail: Condo owners hold fee simple Title to their unit plus an undivided interest in common areas — hallways, lobby, roof, amenities. The HOA collects monthly dues to maintain common areas and enforces CC&Rs. Condos finance like single-family homes (FHA Loan and conventional both available) but Lenders also underwrite the building's financials, owner-occupancy ratio, and reserve adequacy. Contrast with a Co-op.

plain: The process of turning a rental Multifamily building into individually-owned Condo units — Tenants get the right to buy their units, then the rest sell to the open market.
snappy: Process converting a rental Multifamily into individually-owned Condo units.
detail: Condo conversion was a defining urban Real Estate move in the 1970s-1980s and revived periodically in hot markets. Local laws govern the process — Tenant protections (right of first refusal, relocation assistance, senior/disabled exemptions) vary widely. New York City and San Francisco have particularly tight rules. Economics work when Condo retail value per unit exceeds rental Sale Price by enough to cover conversion costs (legal, condo declaration, common-area renovation) and Tenant payouts. Tenants choosing not to buy must vacate or remain under rent-controlled terms depending on jurisdiction.

plain: The recorded master document that creates a Condo association — defines unit boundaries, common areas, voting rights, and the rules under which the association operates.
snappy: Recorded master document creating a Condo association and defining unit/common-area boundaries.
detail: The Condo Declaration is the foundational document, filed with the county recorder when the project is first declared as Condo. It defines: unit boundaries (often the inside surface of perimeter walls), undivided interest in common elements, limited common elements (balconies, parking, storage assigned to specific units), voting weights, restrictions on use. The Bylaws govern association operations. The CC&Rs govern owner conduct. Together, the Declaration, Bylaws, and CC&Rs form 'governing documents' a buyer must review during Due Diligence. Amendments require supermajority owner approval — 75% or higher in most states.

plain: A Mortgage small enough to meet the size limits Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will buy — most everyday US Mortgages.
snappy: Mortgage at or below the size limit Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will purchase.
detail: Conforming Loans meet underwriting and loan-size limits set annually by FHFA. The standard 2024 limit is $766,550 in most US counties, higher in designated high-cost areas. Conforming loans are routinely sold from Lenders to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, packaged into agency MBS, and resold to investors — that liquidity is why conforming rates are cheaper than jumbo. Above the limit it becomes a jumbo loan.

plain: A short-term loan that funds the building of a new property — draws cash as the work progresses.
snappy: Short-term loan disbursing in stages to fund construction.
detail: Construction Loans fund building rather than purchase. Funds release in draws against completed milestones (foundation, framing, drywall, completion), each verified by Inspector visits. Typically 12-24 month terms with interest-only payments on the drawn balance. Higher interest rates than purchase Mortgages reflect construction risk. Construction-to-permanent (one-time-close) loans convert automatically to a standard Mortgage on completion. Builders use construction loans too — separate from end-buyer financing.

plain: A clause in a purchase contract that lets the buyer back out without losing the Earnest Money Deposit if something specific goes wrong.
snappy: Contractual escape hatch tied to a specific condition being met.
detail: Common contingencies include the inspection contingency (buyer can walk if inspection finds problems), the Appraisal Contingency (buyer can walk if the property doesn't appraise at contract price), the financing contingency (buyer can walk if the Lender denies the loan), and the home-sale contingency (buyer can walk if their existing home doesn't sell). Removing contingencies makes an offer more attractive but riskier for the buyer.

plain: A Mortgage that is not government-backed — not an FHA Loan, VA Loan, or USDA Loan. Most US Mortgages are conventional.
snappy: Non-government Mortgage; usually purchased by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.
detail: Conventional Loans contrast with government-backed loans (FHA Loan, VA Loan, USDA). Most are Conforming Loans bought by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; some are non-conforming jumbos held on Lender balance sheets or sold to private investors. Conventional borrowers with Down Payment under 20% pay Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) until they reach 20% Equity. Generally requires higher Credit Score than government-backed alternatives.

plain: A low-risk Real Estate investment strategy targeting stabilised, top-quality property — modest leverage, steady cash flow, single-digit IRR targets.
snappy: Lowest-risk Real Estate strategy — stabilised Class A property, modest leverage, single-digit IRR.
detail: Core sits at the low-risk end of the Real Estate strategy spectrum, alongside Core-Plus (slightly higher risk), Value-Add (moderate-risk Rehab), and Opportunistic (highest-risk development or distressed). Core deals target stabilised Class A property in major markets, leverage at 40-55% LTV, Hold Period 7-10+ years, IRR 7-10% (unlevered) or 8-12% (levered), with most of the return from cash yield rather than appreciation. Pension funds, sovereign wealth, and listed REITs dominate Core capital. Cap Rate Compression hit hardest in Core during 2015-2022.

plain: A Real Estate investment strategy one step riskier than Core — stabilised property with slightly more leverage, value-add potential, or secondary markets.
snappy: Real Estate strategy between Core and Value-Add — stabilised property, moderate leverage.
detail: Core-Plus deals target stabilised property in good condition that has light improvement potential — minor renovation, modest Rent-roll mark-to-market, modest Cap-Ex. Leverage runs 55-65% LTV (above Core's 40-55%). Hold Period 5-10 years. Levered IRR target 10-13%, mostly from cash flow with modest appreciation. Common Core-Plus moves: lease-up a 90% leased Office to 95%, renovate Multifamily Common Areas without unit interiors, rebrand a Hotel. Less risk than Value-Add (no major Rehab or repositioning), more upside than Core.

plain: A smaller bank or Mortgage company that originates and closes loans in its own name — then sells them to a larger 'sponsor' bank shortly after Closing.
snappy: Smaller Lender originating Mortgages in own name, then selling to a sponsor bank post-close.
detail: Correspondent lending is the middle path between Mortgage Banker (holds or sells to GSEs directly) and Mortgage Broker (never funds). The correspondent funds the loan using its own warehouse line, then sells closed loans to a sponsor bank (Wells Fargo, Chase, US Bank, PennyMac) within days or weeks. The sponsor reunderwrites, repurchases unacceptable loans, and either holds or sells onward. Correspondent Lenders gain pricing scale they couldn't reach independently while keeping the relationship with the borrower. Community banks and credit unions often run correspondent operations to keep mortgage operations profitable.

plain: An Appraisal method that values a property as the cost to rebuild it from scratch, minus Depreciation for age and wear, plus Land value.
snappy: Appraisal method valuing improvements at replacement cost less Depreciation plus Land value.
detail: The cost approach works best for new or special-use property: a school, fire station, brand-new build, or unique property with no Comps. The Appraiser estimates the cost to construct an equivalent building today (Replacement Cost) or to reproduce the exact building (reproduction cost), subtracts accrued Depreciation (physical wear, Functional Obsolescence, External Obsolescence), and adds the Land's value to reach total value. For old, conventional property the cost approach is least reliable — accrued Depreciation estimates carry too much error.

plain: A tax study that accelerates Depreciation deductions on a building by reclassifying parts of it as shorter-life assets.
snappy: Engineering study accelerating Depreciation on commercial property assets.
detail: A cost-segregation study breaks a building's purchase price into components with different IRS Depreciation lives — the building shell stays at 27.5 (residential) or 39 (commercial) years, but carpets, fixtures, parking lot, and landscaping qualify for 5-, 7-, or 15-year schedules. Front-loading Depreciation boosts after-tax cash flow in the early years of ownership. Most useful for buildings over $500K. Recapture at sale claws some benefit back.

plain: A seller's modified response to a buyer's offer — usually a different price or terms.
snappy: Modified response to an offer that becomes a new offer requiring acceptance.
detail: A counteroffer legally rejects the original offer and substitutes new terms — the original is dead. The party who counter-offers becomes the new offeror; the other party must accept, counter again, or walk. Counters typically adjust price, Closing date, Contingency timing, or specific concessions like seller-paid Closing Costs. Sophisticated negotiations often involve three or four rounds of counters before signing.

plain: A binding promise written into a Deed or HOA rules — about how the property can be used.
snappy: Recorded promise restricting how a property is used; runs with the land.
detail: Covenants run with the land — every successor owner is bound regardless of whether they were a party to the original agreement. CC&Rs are the most common bundle of covenants in residential subdivisions and condo communities. Older Deeds occasionally contain racially restrictive covenants — these have been federally unenforceable since the 1948 Supreme Court ruling in Shelley v. Kraemer but often survive on paper as historical artefacts.

plain: A three-digit summary of how reliably you've repaid debt — Lenders use it to price your Mortgage.
snappy: Numeric credit-risk score; FICO 300-850 is the dominant US scale.
detail: Mortgage Lenders use FICO scores from all three credit bureaus and typically take the middle score. Conventional Loans usually require 620+; FHA Loans go as low as 580 (or 500 with 10% Down Payment); VA and USDA have no hard minimum but Lenders impose their own (often 620). Higher scores access lower interest rates and lower PMI. A 100-point score difference can mean tens of thousands in lifetime interest.

plain: How attractive a property looks from the street — paint, landscaping, front door — strongly affects sale price.
snappy: First-impression visual appeal of a property from the street.
detail: Curb Appeal is the first signal buyers form about a property before stepping inside. Sellers invest in landscaping, exterior paint, front-door refresh, and tidy walkways to boost it before listing. Empirical studies suggest strong curb appeal lifts sale price 5-7% versus identical homes with poor exteriors. Agents almost universally recommend curb-appeal work as the highest-ROI pre-listing investment.

plain: A house built to the buyer's specific design and specifications — architect-drawn plans, custom finishes, longer build time, premium price.
snappy: House built to buyer-specific design with custom finishes and floor plan.
detail: Custom homes start with an architect (or buyer-purchased plans) and a Lot the buyer typically owns. The builder works on cost-plus, GMP, or stipulated-sum contracts. Timelines: 12-24 months from breaking ground for a true custom build. Cost premium over comparable tract: 30-100%, depending on market and finish level. Common reasons buyers go custom: specific Lot constraints (slope, view, water access), specific design preferences (architectural style, layout), or specific finish quality (high-end mechanical, premium materials). Cost overrun risk is the buyer's primary friction — change orders are expensive.

plain: How long a property has been listed for sale — a key signal of pricing and demand.
snappy: Calendar days since a property hit the market.
detail: DOM tracks calendar days from MLS listing date to contract acceptance. Hot markets see medians under 7 days; slow markets stretch to 60-90+. Days on Market is one of the most-watched market-temperature signals — alongside list-to-sale ratio and inventory months supply. Re-listing tricks (cancel and relist to reset DOM) are widely used and partially defeated by MLS rules tracking cumulative DOM across re-listings.

plain: Common shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow — the valuation method projecting future cash flows and discounting them back to present value.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow in valuation.
detail: DCF is universal industry shorthand for Discounted Cash Flow analysis. Real Estate analysts and institutional investors cite 'the DCF' as shorthand for the underwriting model itself. See Discounted Cash Flow for the methodology, sensitivities to Exit Cap Rate and discount rate, and how DCF compares to direct capitalisation as a valuation approach for stabilised property.

plain: The full spelling of DTI — the monthly-debt-to-monthly-income ratio Lenders use to size a Mortgage.
snappy: Full spelling of DTI — the borrower's debt-to-income ratio.
detail: Debt-to-Income Ratio is the formal spelling of DTI, the headline qualification metric for residential Mortgage underwriting. Two flavours: front-end (housing-only, typically capped 28%) and back-end (all debt, typically capped 36-45% depending on program). Higher ratios may clear with compensating factors — reserves, a high Credit Score, or a large Down Payment. See DTI for the operational mechanics; this entry exists so prose written out longhand also auto-links.

plain: The legal document that transfers ownership of a property from seller to buyer — signed at Closing and filed with the county.
snappy: Written instrument conveying real-property Title between parties.
detail: A deed transfers ownership from grantor to grantee. The instrument must be written, identify the parties and property, contain words of conveyance, and be signed by the grantor. Common types: warranty deed (full Title guarantees), special warranty deed (limited guarantees), Quitclaim Deed (no guarantees — common in divorce or family transfers), and Deed of Trust (used in place of a Mortgage in many states). Deeds must be recorded with the county to give public notice.

plain: When a struggling borrower hands the property back to the Lender voluntarily instead of going through Foreclosure.
snappy: Voluntary transfer of Deed to Lender to avoid Foreclosure.
detail: A deed in lieu is a workout: rather than fight the Foreclosure process, the borrower deeds the property directly to the Lender in exchange for cancellation of the Mortgage debt. Faster and cheaper than Foreclosure for both sides, and less damaging to the borrower's Credit Score. The Lender must accept — they may refuse if junior Liens or other encumbrances complicate Title. Tax: forgiven debt can be taxable income, though some federal exclusions apply.

plain: An alternative to a Mortgage used in many US states — a third party (trustee) holds Title until the loan is paid.
snappy: Three-party security instrument with a trustee holding Title until payoff.
detail: States divide between Mortgage states and Deed of Trust states. In a Deed of Trust state (California, Texas, Virginia, and most of the West), the borrower conveys Title to a trustee who holds it for the Lender. On Default, the trustee can foreclose non-judicially — faster and cheaper than the judicial Foreclosure required in Mortgage states. Functionally equivalent to a Mortgage from the borrower's perspective.

plain: Failing to keep up with Mortgage payments or otherwise breaching the loan agreement.
snappy: Breach of the Mortgage contract, usually missed payments.
detail: Default is the breach that triggers the Acceleration Clause and ultimately Foreclosure. Most Mortgages enter technical default after 30 days late and serious default after 90. Lenders generally try to work with borrowers (forbearance, loan modification, short sale) before foreclosing because foreclosure is costly and produces a discounted REO sale. Loan loss provisioning and CMBS investor reporting use specific 60+ and 90+ day default metrics.

plain: The yearly tax deduction investors take to reflect that a building wears out — even though most rise in market value.
snappy: Annual tax deduction for the wear-and-tear of an income property.
detail: The IRS treats every commercial building as wearing out over 39 years and every residential rental over 27.5 years (the land underneath isn't depreciable). The annual deduction reduces taxable income from rent without an actual cash expense — a major reason real-estate investment is tax-favoured. Cost Segregation accelerates the timeline by reclassifying components. Depreciation taken is recaptured at 25% federal when the property is sold, unless rolled into a 1031 Exchange.

plain: A tax claw-back at the Sale of a depreciated property — gains attributable to prior Depreciation deductions are taxed at a higher rate than long-term Capital Gain.
snappy: Tax claw-back at sale on gain previously deducted as Depreciation, at elevated rates.
detail: When a depreciated property sells, IRS recharacterises a portion of the gain as ordinary depreciation recapture rather than long-term Capital Gain. For Real Property under §1250, the recapture rate is capped at 25%. For personal-property components (carpeting, appliances, parking lot improvements identified through Cost Segregation) under §1245, recapture is at full ordinary rates — up to 37%. 1031 Exchange defers depreciation recapture along with Capital Gain. Step-up in Basis at death eliminates both.

plain: When buyer and seller use different Agents inside the same brokerage — the alternative to Dual Agency.
snappy: Separate Agents inside one brokerage representing buyer and seller.
detail: Designated Agency lets two Agents in the same brokerage represent opposing parties in a single transaction. Each owes fiduciary duty to their client; the Broker walks a neutral line above them. Adopted in many states as a less-conflicted alternative to Dual Agency. Critics argue Broker-level loyalty conflicts persist; defenders argue agent-level separation provides meaningful client advocacy. Real estate Commission economics typically remain unchanged from a single-brokerage transaction.

plain: Written information the seller must give the buyer about known defects, hazards, or material facts.
snappy: Seller's required written statement of known property issues.
detail: Most US states require sellers to fill out a disclosure form covering known issues — roof leaks, foundation cracks, mould, neighbour disputes, pending litigation, lead paint (mandatory federal disclosure for pre-1978 homes), and similar. The standard is what the seller actually knew, not what they should have noticed. Buyers who later discover an undisclosed material defect can sue for damages. Inspector findings supplement disclosure but don't replace it.

plain: Upfront fees you pay the Lender at Closing to permanently lower your Mortgage's interest rate.
snappy: Prepaid Interest fee at Closing, each point ~1% of loan size for ~0.25% rate cut.
detail: One discount point equals 1% of the loan amount and typically reduces the interest rate by 0.25%, though the exact ratio varies by Lender and market. Points are a form of Buy-Down: paying for a lower rate over the life of the loan. The break-even depends on how long the borrower keeps the Mortgage — generally 5-7 years to recover the upfront cost via lower monthly Interest. Disclosed on the Loan Estimate and rolled into APR.

plain: A valuation method that projects every year's cash flow and the exit Sale Price, then discounts them back to present value using a target return rate.
snappy: Valuation method discounting projected cash flows back to present value at a target rate.
detail: DCF dominates institutional Commercial Real Estate underwriting. The model projects 5-10 years of annual NOI (after Cap-Ex and Replacement Reserve), an Exit Cap Rate applied to year-N+1 NOI for reversion value, and discounts every cash flow back at a target unlevered return (often 7-12% depending on risk). The IRR that makes NPV equal zero is the deal's projected return. DCF is more sensitive than direct capitalisation to: Rent growth assumptions, Exit Cap Rate, discount rate. Sensitivity tables surround the base case. The Income Approach uses DCF as its primary methodology for stabilised property.

plain: A property whose owner can no longer service the debt or operate it profitably — opportunities for buyers with capital and patience to acquire below replacement cost.
snappy: Property whose owner can't service debt or operate profitably — discount buying opportunity.
detail: Distressed assets surface in down cycles. Causes: maturity defaults (loan comes due in a high-rate environment, can't refinance), operating shortfalls (vacancy, declining Rents), sponsor mismanagement, structural obsolescence. The acquisition path varies. Direct purchase from the owner at distressed pricing. Note acquisition from the Lender (buy the Mortgage, then negotiate with the borrower or foreclose). Foreclosure auction. Deed in Lieu negotiations. REO purchases after Foreclosure. Distressed cycles (1990 Resolution Trust, 2008-2012, 2023-2024 office) generate the largest one-time Real Estate fortunes — and the largest losses for sellers.

plain: Common shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Act — the 2010 financial-reform law that reshaped Mortgage lending.
snappy: Standard shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform Act.
detail: Dodd-Frank is the industry shorthand for the Dodd-Frank Act, named after Senator Chris Dodd and Representative Barney Frank. The shorthand dominates day-to-day conversation in Mortgage compliance and consumer-finance circles. See Dodd-Frank Act for the substantive mortgage-lending provisions: CFPB creation, Qualified Mortgage rules, ability-to-repay, Loan Officer compensation restrictions.

full: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
plain: The 2010 financial-reform law that created the CFPB and overhauled Mortgage lending rules after the 2008 crisis.
snappy: 2010 financial-reform statute creating the CFPB and rewriting mortgage origination rules.
detail: Dodd-Frank tightened residential Mortgage lending after the 2008 collapse. Created the CFPB and gave it rule-writing authority. Imposed the ability-to-repay rule and the Qualified Mortgage safe harbour (DTI cap, no risky features). Restricted Loan Officer compensation to prevent steering. Created mandatory escrows for higher-priced loans. Imposed risk-retention on private MBS issuers. The statute is sprawling; most retail-side impact for Real Estate flows through CFPB regulations (TRID, Reg Z, Reg X).

plain: The cash you put down upfront when buying a home — the rest is the Mortgage.
snappy: Cash paid by the buyer at Closing, with the Lender financing the balance.
detail: Conventional Loans typically require 5-20% down; FHA Loans allow 3.5% with mortgage insurance; VA Loans and USDA Loans permit zero down for eligible borrowers. A 20% Down Payment lets Conventional borrowers avoid PMI and often unlocks better pricing tiers. Down Payment combined with LTV defines the borrower's initial Equity. Larger down payments increase loan approval odds and reduce interest rate.

plain: For investment properties — how many times the rental income covers the Mortgage payment.
snappy: NOI divided by annual debt service — coverage cushion on a commercial loan.
detail: DSCR is the commercial real estate analogue of Debt-to-Income Ratio. NOI divided by annual debt service: 1.20 means the property generates 20% more income than required to cover the Mortgage. Most commercial Lenders require 1.20-1.25 minimum at Underwriting.
