DSCR loans for single-family rentals exploded post-2020 — they qualify the borrower based on the property's rent rather than personal income.

plain: Your monthly debt payments divided by your monthly income — Lenders cap how high it can go to qualify.
snappy: Monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income.
detail: Lenders compute two DTIs: front-end (Mortgage payment, Property Tax, insurance, HOA divided by income) and back-end (all of the above plus car loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments). Most Conforming Loans cap back-end DTI at 43-45%, though Conventional Loan AUS approvals stretch to 50%. DTI is the single biggest determinant of Mortgage qualification alongside Credit Score.

plain: When one agent or brokerage represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction.
snappy: Single agent or Broker representing both buyer and seller in one deal.
detail: Dual Agency creates an inherent conflict — the agent owes fiduciary duties to both sides simultaneously. Some states ban it outright; others allow it with written disclosure and informed consent. Critics argue it incentivises closing the deal over advocating for either party. A variant — designated agency — assigns different agents within the same brokerage to each side, narrowing the conflict to the Broker level.

plain: The investigation period after going under contract — inspections, document review, surveys — before the deal closes.
snappy: Investigation period during which the buyer verifies the property and its records.
detail: In residential transactions, due diligence runs through the Contingency periods — typically 7-14 days for inspection, 14-21 for Appraisal. The buyer hires professionals (Inspector, Appraiser, surveyor) and reviews documents (HOA financials, CC&Rs, Title Insurance commitment, lead-paint disclosure). Commercial due diligence is longer (30-90 days) and broader: phase I environmental, tenant interviews, lease audit, market study. Findings drive renegotiation or termination via Contingency.

plain: Cash you put down with your offer to show the seller you're serious — applied to the purchase if the deal closes.
snappy: Good-faith deposit accompanying a purchase offer; credited at Closing.
detail: Earnest Money signals commitment. Typically 1-3% of price in normal markets, 5-10% in competitive ones. EMD is held in Escrow by the Broker, attorney, or title company. If the buyer terminates within Contingency periods (inspection, Appraisal, financing), the EMD is refunded. Walking away after Contingencies expire generally forfeits the EMD to the seller as liquidated damages.

plain: A right to use part of someone else's Land for a specific purpose — like a shared driveway or a utility line.
snappy: Limited right to use another party's Real Property for a defined purpose.
detail: Easements run with the Land — they bind future owners, not just the current one. Common types: utility easements (power, water, sewer), access easements (driveways crossing a neighbour's Lot), conservation easements (restricting development). Created by Deed, prescription (long use, like Adverse Possession), or necessity (landlocked parcels). Title Insurance and Inspections should surface recorded easements; unrecorded prescriptive easements are a litigation risk. A holder who oversteps the scope becomes a trespasser.

plain: The federal law banning Lender discrimination based on race, religion, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance — applies to Mortgages and all consumer credit.
snappy: Federal anti-discrimination law in lending — covers all protected classes in credit.
detail: Enacted 1974, codified at 15 USC §1691, implemented by CFPB's Regulation B. ECOA covers any extension of credit — Mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, business loans. Prohibited factors: race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (over 18), receipt of public-assistance income, exercise of consumer-protection rights. The CFPB has brought Redlining cases under ECOA against banks for branch placement, marketing, and Underwriting that disproportionately exclude minority neighbourhoods. Adverse-action notices required when an application is denied — listing specific reasons.

plain: An Appraiser's judgment of a property's apparent age — based on condition and modernisation — rather than its calendar age.
snappy: Apparent age judged from condition and updates, distinct from chronological age.
detail: A 1950 house gutted and modernised in 2022 might have an effective age of 5 years even though chronological age is 75. Effective Age drives the Depreciation deduction in the Cost Approach. A 1990 commercial building that has been kept in showroom condition could have effective age of 15; a poorly maintained 2010 building could have effective age of 25. Appraisers reconcile effective age against the property's economic life (typical service life for the type) to estimate accrued Depreciation as a percentage.

plain: The property's actual collected Rent — Gross Rental Income minus what's lost to vacancy, concessions, and bad debt.
snappy: Gross Rental Income minus vacancy, concessions, and collection loss.
detail: EGI is the realistic top line of a property's income statement, sitting between Gross Rental Income (theoretical full-Rent at full occupancy) and NOI (after Operating Expenses). The gap between GRI and EGI shows up as the 'vacancy and collection loss' line — typically 5-10% in stabilised Multifamily, more in turnover-heavy or concession-driven markets. Sloppy underwriting confuses EGI and GRI; the latter inflates NOI by the vacancy adjustment that should sit between.

plain: When a structure or improvement crosses the property line onto a neighbour's Land — a fence, an overhanging eave, an extending driveway.
snappy: Physical intrusion of a structure or improvement onto neighbouring property.
detail: An encroachment is a survey problem with legal teeth. Even a few inches can complicate Title Insurance, frustrate Sale, or — left long enough — ripen into Adverse Possession against the original owner. Common culprits: fences built without surveys, additions extending past setbacks, roof overhangs, driveways. Discovered through a current Survey (often required by Lenders). Remedies: removal, monetary settlement, granting an Easement to legalise the encroachment, or buying the affected strip of Land.

plain: Any legal claim or restriction on a property that limits what the owner can do — a Mortgage, Lien, Easement, or use restriction.
snappy: Any third-party claim or restriction on Real Property that limits the owner's rights.
detail: Encumbrances split into financial claims (Mortgage, Lien) and use restrictions (Easement, CC&Rs, lease, Zoning overlays). Title searches and Title Insurance focus on disclosing all recorded encumbrances before Closing. Not every encumbrance kills a deal — buyers expect to take property subject to utility easements and CC&Rs. But undisclosed encumbrances (an old judgment Lien from a prior owner) are the kind of defect Title Insurance is built to cover. Sellers warrant the property free of undisclosed encumbrances in a Warranty Deed.

plain: What you actually own of your home — the gap between its current value and what you still owe on the Mortgage.
snappy: Owner's share — current value minus outstanding Mortgage balance.
detail: Equity equals current market value minus all outstanding debt secured against the property. A $500K home with a $300K Mortgage balance produces $200K in Equity. Equity builds two ways: Principal paydown via Amortization, and market appreciation. Owners tap Equity through cash-out Refinance, home Equity loans (a second mortgage), or HELOCs. Equity is the foundation of personal household wealth in the US — for most owners, it dwarfs other assets.

plain: How many times the investor gets their money back over the deal's life — a 2.0x equity multiple means doubling the original investment.
snappy: Total distributions divided by total invested equity over the holding period.
detail: Equity multiple is IRR's plain-English cousin. It ignores timing — a 2.0x over five years and a 2.0x over fifteen years look identical on equity multiple but very different on IRR. Both metrics get reported side-by-side in syndication offering memos. Typical Multifamily value-add targets: 1.7–2.2x equity multiple alongside 15–20% IRR. Core deals target 1.4–1.7x at 8–12% IRR. The metric is intuitive to first-time investors who get confused by IRR's compounding math.

plain: A Lease provision that automatically bumps Rent up over time — fixed steps, CPI, or market-driven.
snappy: Lease provision raising Rent annually by a fixed amount, CPI, or market.
detail: Three common escalation structures. (1) Fixed steps: Rent rises a set dollar or percentage amount each year ($1/PSF, or 3%). Predictable for both parties. (2) CPI-linked: annual bumps tied to Consumer Price Index, sometimes capped. Inflation hedge for Landlord. (3) Market-based: periodic resets to market Rent, sometimes with collar/cap. Common in long-term ground leases. Multifamily Leases often skip Escalation Clauses since terms are short (12 months) and the entire Rent resets at renewal. Commercial Leases of 5-10+ years rely heavily on Escalations to grow NOI.

plain: A neutral third party that holds money or documents on behalf of the buyer and seller until the deal closes.
snappy: Third-party holding of funds or documents pending Closing.
detail: Escrow holds the Earnest Money Deposit, Closing funds, and Deed between contract and Closing — releasing each only when the conditions are met. After Closing, many Mortgages keep an escrow account that collects monthly Property Tax and insurance premiums alongside the loan payment, then disburses them when due. Lenders typically require escrow accounts when LTV exceeds 80%.

plain: A signed Tenant document confirming key Lease terms — Rent paid, no defaults, no special claims against the Landlord — required at building sale or refinance.
snappy: Tenant-signed certificate confirming Lease terms and stopping later claims that contradict it.
detail: Estoppel certificates protect the buyer or new Lender from surprise post-Closing claims by Tenants. The certificate confirms: current Rent, remaining term, options and renewal rights, no Landlord defaults, no offsets, no oral side agreements, no claims for repairs. Once signed, the Tenant is 'estopped' (legally prevented) from making contradictory claims later. Mandatory at sale of investment property — Lenders won't fund without them from major Tenants. Tenants negotiate certain estoppel exclusions (preserve audit rights, environmental claims). Multifamily transactions sometimes use 'tenant questionnaires' instead.

plain: The legal process Landlords use to remove a Tenant who has stopped paying rent or breached the Lease.
snappy: Court-ordered removal of a Tenant from a leased property.
detail: Eviction is a court process — Landlords cannot self-help by changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities. Steps: written notice (3-30 days depending on state and grounds), filing an unlawful-detainer action, court hearing, judgment, and sheriff-enforced removal. Total time runs from 3 weeks (fast states like Texas) to 6+ months (slow states like New York). Tenants can typically cure non-payment evictions by paying owed rent before judgment.

plain: The Cap Rate assumed at sale at the end of the hold period — drives the projected Sale Price in any underwriting model.
snappy: Cap Rate assumed at projected exit sale, driving the residual value.
detail: Exit cap rate is the most sensitive assumption in any commercial Real Estate underwrite. A 25-basis-point change in Exit Cap moves residual value by 4-5% — enough to flip a deal from win to loss. Conservative underwriting prices Exit Cap above Going-In Cap Rate to reflect normal Cap Rate widening over a typical 5-7 year hold. Aggressive underwriting holds Exit Cap flat or compresses it — a red flag in pro formas. Sensitivity tables in offering memos quantify the range; LPs scrutinise.

plain: A loss in property value caused by factors outside the property — a noisy highway next door, a dying retail strip, a declining neighbourhood — that the owner can't fix.
snappy: Loss in property value from factors outside the property the owner can't change.
detail: External obsolescence is the third leg of Depreciation alongside physical wear and Functional Obsolescence. Examples: a new highway built behind a residential subdivision, an industrial plant moved next door to apartments, a regional employer's relocation gutting demand, neighbourhood decline pushing comparable values down. Always incurable from the property's perspective — the Appraiser deducts it as a value loss in the Cost Approach. The Income Approach and Sales Comparison Approach naturally pick up external obsolescence through depressed rents and falling Comps.

plain: The 1968 federal law banning housing discrimination on race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, disability, and family status.
snappy: 1968 federal law banning housing discrimination on protected classes.
detail: The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in renting, selling, financing, and advertising housing based on race, colour, religion, national origin, sex, disability, and family status (the seven federal protected classes). Many states and cities add classes — sexual orientation, gender identity, source of income, military status. HUD's Office of Fair Housing investigates complaints. Lenders, Landlords, and real estate Agents face civil and criminal liability for violations.

plain: The largest US government-sponsored buyer of home loans — Lenders sell Mortgages to Fannie Mae and Fannie repackages them for investors.
snappy: Government-sponsored enterprise that buys Conforming Loans from Lenders.
detail: Fannie Mae is a publicly traded but federally chartered company (a government-sponsored enterprise, or GSE) that buys Conforming Loans from Lenders, repackages them into mortgage-backed securities, and sells those to investors. This secondary market provides the liquidity that lets Lenders keep originating new Mortgages. Fannie Mae went into federal conservatorship in 2008 and remains there. Sister entity Freddie Mac plays the same role with slightly different operational rules.

plain: Common shorthand for Floor Area Ratio — the multiplier of Lot size that caps total building floor area under Zoning.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Floor Area Ratio in Zoning analysis.
detail: FAR is the Zoning vocabulary for building density. Pronounced 'far' as one syllable in industry use. Cities publish FAR caps by district — Manhattan downtown FAR can exceed 15; suburban Office parks run 0.3-0.5. Higher-FAR Zoning multiplies Land value because more revenue-generating square footage can fit on the same parcel. See Floor Area Ratio for full mechanics, bonus structures, and how FAR interacts with Setback and height limits.

plain: The most complete form of ownership — you can use the Land, sell it, leave it to heirs, with no time limit.
snappy: Absolute ownership of Real Property with no time limit and full transfer rights.
detail: Fee simple is the default form of US Real Property ownership. The holder can occupy, sell, mortgage, lease, or devise the property without expiration. Restrictions still apply: Zoning, Property Tax, Easements, CC&Rs, and Eminent Domain all bind a fee simple owner. Compare leasehold (a tenant under a Lease has possession but not ownership) and life estate (ownership ends at the holder's death). Almost all single-family homes in the US are sold fee simple.

plain: The federal agency inside HUD that insures FHA Loans, letting buyers get a Mortgage with only 3.5% down.
snappy: Federal agency inside HUD insuring low-Down-Payment FHA Loans.
detail: The FHA insures Mortgages made to low-Down-Payment borrowers, letting them buy with as little as 3.5% down (or 10% down with Credit Score 500-579). The insurance — funded by borrower-paid MIP — covers Lender losses on Default, which is why Lenders accept lower Credit Scores and Down Payments on an FHA Loan than on a Conventional Loan. Part of HUD; distinct from FHFA (which oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac).

plain: A Mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration — easier to qualify for and lower Down Payment than conventional.
snappy: FHA-insured Mortgage with 3.5% Down Payment minimum.
detail: FHA Loans require 3.5% Down Payment with a Credit Score of 580+, or 10% down with scores 500-579. Borrowers pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium (1.75% of loan amount) and an ongoing monthly premium for the life of the loan if Down Payment is under 10%. Loan limits track FHFA Conforming Loan limits but adjusted by county. FHA Loans are Assumable, which became newly valuable after the 2022 rate spike.

plain: The federal regulator that oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — sets the size limits on Conforming Loans.
snappy: Federal regulator of Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Conforming Loan limits.
detail: The FHFA was created in 2008 to oversee the housing GSEs (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) plus the Federal Home Loan Banks. It sets the annual Conforming Loan limits, supervises the GSEs' Underwriting standards, and acts as their conservator since the 2008 financial crisis. Publishes the closely-watched FHFA House Price Index quarterly, a key benchmark for residential price trends.

plain: The most widely used Credit Score in US lending — a number from 300 to 850 that summarises a borrower's credit history.
snappy: Industry-standard Credit Score model used by most US mortgage lenders.
detail: FICO scores aggregate five factors: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), credit mix (10%). Mortgage underwriting typically pulls FICO from all three bureaus and uses the middle score for the highest-scoring borrower on the application. Conventional Loans usually need 620+; FHA Loans accept 580+ with 3.5% Down Payment, or 500+ with 10%; VA Loans have no statutory minimum but lender overlays often require 620. Higher scores unlock lower rates and lower PMI premiums.

plain: A Mortgage whose interest rate stays the same for the entire loan term — payment never changes.
snappy: Mortgage with a constant interest rate over the full term.
detail: The 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage is the dominant US Mortgage product, available because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy them and bear the prepayment risk. Other terms are 10, 15, 20, and 25 years. The borrower's monthly Principal and Interest payment never changes — only the Property Tax and insurance held in Escrow and insurance adjust. Contrast with an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage, which is cheaper upfront but variable.

plain: An item once Personal Property that's been so attached to a building it now counts as part of the Real Property.
snappy: Personal Property that's been affixed to Real Property and now travels with it.
detail: A ceiling fan was personal property in the box at the hardware store. Once wired into the joists, courts treat it as a fixture — it stays with the house when sold. Common disputes: chandeliers, built-in bookshelves, mounted televisions, washer/dryer hookups. Three-part test: method of attachment, adaptation to the property, intent at the time of installation. Purchase contracts list specific items to exclude (often the kitchen refrigerator) or include to avoid post-Closing arguments.

plain: Insurance covering damage from flooding — usually separate from standard Homeowners Insurance, mostly provided by the federal National Flood Insurance Program in high-risk zones.
snappy: Standalone insurance covering flood damage — mostly federal NFIP in FEMA-mapped flood zones.
detail: Homeowners Insurance excludes flood damage. The federal NFIP (1968) provides most US flood insurance, capped at $250K residential dwelling / $100K contents. Premiums historically set well below true risk — politically subsidised — but FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 (2021) reset premiums toward actuarial pricing, sharply raising rates for older coastal properties. Private flood policies exist for higher coverage limits and luxury homes outside NFIP caps. Required by Lenders for Mortgages on properties in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas. The 2017-2024 hurricane and inland-flood cycle accelerated NFIP losses and reform pressure.

plain: How much total building floor area can fit on a Lot, expressed as a multiplier of Lot size — FAR 2.0 means 200% of the Lot area can be built as floor space across all stories.
snappy: Ratio of buildable floor area to Lot size, set by Zoning.
detail: FAR is the headline density control in urban Zoning. A 10,000 sq ft Lot with FAR 2.0 permits 20,000 sq ft of total floor area — could be 2 stories full-coverage, 4 stories at half-coverage, or some mix. Higher FAR means taller, denser buildings. Manhattan downtown FAR can exceed 15; suburban office parks run 0.3-0.5. Bonuses can lift base FAR (affordable-housing inclusion, public-space contribution, transit proximity). Developers maximise FAR to maximise per-Lot value — the metric drives Land prices in dense markets.

plain: A temporary pause or reduction in Mortgage payments granted by the Lender during a borrower hardship — repayment is deferred but still owed.
snappy: Temporary lender-approved pause or reduction in Mortgage payments during borrower hardship.
detail: Forbearance differs from Loan Modification — it's temporary, not permanent. Common in three scenarios: natural disaster (federal disaster declarations trigger automatic forbearance offers from federally backed Loans), economic shock (the 2020 CARES Act allowed up to 18 months of forbearance on federally backed Mortgages), individual hardship (job loss, medical). Repayment options at the end: lump sum (rarely used), repayment plan (catch-up over months), Loan Modification rolling missed payments into Principal, partial claim (FHA buys back missed payments). Credit reporting is paused or suppressed during the forbearance.

plain: The legal process by which a Lender takes back a property after the borrower stops paying the Mortgage.
snappy: Legal process Lenders use to repossess and sell property after Default.
detail: Foreclosure is triggered by the Acceleration Clause after sustained Default. In Mortgage states, foreclosure is judicial — Lenders sue in court and the process takes 12-24 months on average. In Deed of Trust states the process is non-judicial — the trustee can sell at auction in 3-6 months. After auction, unsold properties become REO on the Lender's books. Foreclosure devastates Credit Scores and bars new federally backed Mortgages for 3-7 years.

plain: Fannie Mae's sister GSE — buys Conforming Loans from Lenders and resells them to investors, keeping the Mortgage market liquid.
snappy: Government-sponsored enterprise that buys Conforming Loans, alongside Fannie Mae.
detail: Freddie Mac is the second of the two big housing GSEs alongside Fannie Mae. Created in 1970 to compete with Fannie Mae and add liquidity to the Mortgage market. Buys Conforming Loans from Lenders, securitises them, and publishes the Primary Mortgage Market Survey — the weekly 30-year average rate widely cited in the press. Like Fannie Mae, has been in FHFA conservatorship since 2008.

plain: A loss in property value caused by outdated design, layout, or features — galleys kitchens, low ceilings, no garage, single bathrooms — that buyers no longer want.
snappy: Loss in property value from outdated design, layout, or features inside the building.
detail: Functional obsolescence is the design-side cousin of physical Depreciation. Examples: 8-foot ceilings when the market expects 9-foot, single bathrooms in 4-bedroom homes, drive-through tellers in renovated banks turned offices, narrow Office floor plates that don't suit open-plan layouts, awkward elevator location. Curable functional obsolescence (the cost to fix is less than the value gained) gets accounted for as a renovation budget. Incurable functional obsolescence (cost exceeds gain) gets deducted as a value loss. Distinct from External Obsolescence (which comes from outside the property).

plain: Common shorthand for a General Contractor — the firm managing all construction work on a project.
snappy: Standard shorthand for General Contractor in construction.
detail: GC is the universal industry shorthand for General Contractor. Owners, architects, Lenders, and Subcontractors all refer to the GC in daily conversation and contract language. See General Contractor for the substantive role, contract structures (stipulated sum, cost-plus, GMP), and how the GC coordinates Subcontractors and certifies progress payments.

plain: The firm hired by the property owner or developer to manage all construction work — coordinates subcontractors, handles permits, delivers the completed building.
snappy: Firm managing all construction work — coordinates Subcontractors and delivers the building.
detail: GCs structure construction projects in one of three ways. Stipulated sum: fixed contract price (low risk to owner, GC absorbs cost overruns). Cost-plus: actual costs reimbursed plus a fee (more transparent, owner bears overrun risk). Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP): cost-plus with a cap (hybrid). The GC schedules trades (framing, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, finishes), pulls permits, manages inspections, certifies progress payments, manages punch lists. Bonded GCs carry payment and performance bonds protecting the owner if work isn't completed. Pre-construction services are often a separate engagement before the build contract.

plain: A federal agency that guarantees mortgage-backed securities made of FHA, VA, and USDA loans — full faith and credit of the US government.
snappy: Federal guarantor of MBS made from FHA, VA, USDA loan pools.
detail: Unlike Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (privately owned GSEs), Ginnie Mae is a wholly federal agency inside HUD. It does not buy loans — instead it guarantees the timely payment of mortgage-backed securities made of government-insured loans (FHA Loan, VA Loan, USDA Loan). The full-faith-and-credit guarantee gives Ginnie MBS the lowest credit risk in the agency MBS space, just above US Treasuries.

plain: A construction contract structure where the GC commits to a maximum price — overruns above that cap fall on the contractor, savings below it usually share with the owner.
snappy: Construction contract with GC-committed price cap and shared-savings split.
detail: GMP contracts (Guaranteed Maximum Price) bridge stipulated-sum and cost-plus. The GC opens its books to the owner (transparent cost reporting) but commits to a maximum price ceiling. Cost overruns above the GMP eat into the GC's fee or come out of contractor pocket. Cost savings below the GMP are shared, typically 50/50 or 75/25 owner-favoured. Used in complex commercial projects where neither stipulated sum (too risky for GC given pricing uncertainty) nor cost-plus (too risky for owner) fits. Pre-construction services and trade buyout transparency are essential to GMP success.

plain: The Cap Rate at the moment of acquisition — calculated from the in-place NOI divided by the purchase price.
snappy: Cap Rate at purchase: current NOI divided by Sale Price.
detail: Going-in cap rate is the snapshot of yield at acquisition. A 5.5% going-in cap on a Multifamily deal means $5.50 of NOI per $100 of purchase price. Value-add Sponsors target a going-in cap below the Exit Cap Rate — they accept lower yield at purchase, expect to lift NOI through Rehab and re-tenanting, and exit at a higher NOI even at a higher Exit Cap. Going-in cap rates compress when investor capital floods in (2020-2021); they widen when rates rise (2022 onward).

plain: The pre-TRID disclosure form giving borrowers an early estimate of Closing Costs — now replaced by the Loan Estimate for residential loans.
snappy: Pre-2015 mortgage cost disclosure, replaced by the Loan Estimate under TRID.
detail: From 1974 (RESPA) until October 2015, lenders had to give a Good Faith Estimate within three business days of application — itemising every Closing Cost. The TRID rule consolidated GFE and the early TILA disclosure into the Loan Estimate. Commercial Real Estate loans, reverse mortgages, and certain home-equity loans still use GFE-style disclosures. The term remains common shorthand in industry conversation even though the form itself is retired for most residential business.

plain: Common shorthand for the General Partner — the Sponsor running a Real Estate syndication.
snappy: Standard shorthand for the active Sponsor in a Real Estate syndication.
detail: GP is shorthand for General Partner — the active partner in a limited-partnership or LLC structure. In Real Estate parlance the GP and Sponsor are interchangeable terms. The GP holds operational control, signs personal guarantees on Recourse Loans, and earns the Promote above the Preferred Return. GPs face fiduciary duties to LPs that are often modified by the partnership agreement; some structures use waivers that LPs scrutinise carefully. See Sponsor for the broader role.

plain: The party transferring ownership in a Deed — typically the seller.
snappy: Party conveying property in a Deed transaction; the seller.
detail: Grantor and grantee are the technical Deed-language terms. The grantor signs the Deed transferring Title; the grantee receives. In a standard purchase, grantor = seller and grantee = buyer. Other contexts: a parent gifting property to children, where the parent is the grantor; a Trust receiving property, where the prior owner is the grantor. The Deed itself must clearly identify both parties to be valid for recording.

plain: A commercial Lease where the Landlord pays all Operating Expenses out of the Rent — the Tenant just pays the headline number.
snappy: Commercial Lease where the Landlord absorbs all Operating Expenses out of base Rent.
detail: Gross leases are common in Office buildings, especially Class A urban towers. The Tenant pays a single all-in Rent; the Landlord covers Property Tax, insurance, utilities, janitorial, repairs. Year-over-year cost increases hit the Landlord. To protect against that, gross leases often include expense stops — the Tenant absorbs operating-cost increases above a base-year benchmark. Compare Triple Net Lease (Tenant pays nets) and Modified Gross (split).

plain: The total Rent a property would collect if every unit were occupied at market rate — before any vacancies or expenses.
snappy: Potential Rent at full occupancy and market rates, before vacancy and expenses.
detail: Gross rental income is the top line of the property income statement. Subtract vacancy and collection loss to get effective gross income. Then subtract Operating Expenses to get NOI. The gap between gross and effective is the property's economic occupancy — physical occupancy minus concessions, bad debt, and below-market leases. Underwriting models flag concession-driven vacancy as a value risk: a property running 95% physical occupancy but giving two months free per Lease has effective economic occupancy closer to 80%.

plain: A private company with a federal charter — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are the two big housing GSEs.
snappy: Federally chartered private company; Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are the housing GSEs.
detail: A GSE is a private corporation with a federal charter and an implicit (or, post-2008, near-explicit) federal backstop. Two GSEs dominate US housing finance — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — both in FHFA conservatorship since 2008. Ginnie Mae is not a GSE (it is a wholly federal agency). The GSE model concentrates housing finance risk on a few large entities, the source of intense post-crisis policy debate.

plain: A short-term, high-Interest loan from a private Lender — used by investors who need speed, not the best rate.
snappy: Short-term, asset-based loan from a private lender at high Interest rates.
detail: Hard money lenders care about the property, not the borrower's W-2. Decisions in days, fund in weeks, with LTV typically capped at 65–75% of After-Repair Value (ARV). Rates run 8–15% with 2–4 points up front. Used by fix-and-flip investors, BRRRR strategists, and developers who need bridge financing while a project gets permitted or stabilised. Terms run 6–24 months. Bank takeouts replace hard money once the property is stabilised and qualifies for conventional financing.

plain: A revolving credit line secured by the home — borrow what you need, pay it down, borrow again, up to a set limit.
snappy: Revolving credit line secured by the Equity in a primary residence.
detail: A HELOC has a draw period (usually 10 years) when the borrower pulls funds and pays interest-only on what's drawn. Then a repayment period (10–20 years) when no new draws are allowed and Principal amortises. Rates are usually variable, tied to the prime rate plus a Margin. Common uses: home improvements, debt consolidation, education, emergency reserves. Lender ratios typically permit combined-LTV up to 80–90% (first Mortgage + HELOC vs. Appraised Value). The home backs the debt — Default risks Foreclosure.

plain: The Appraiser's judgment of the most profitable, physically possible, and legally permitted use of a property — sometimes different from how it's used today.
snappy: Most profitable, possible, legal, and supported use of a property as judged by the Appraiser.
detail: Highest and Best Use governs the entire Appraisal. Four tests: physically possible (Lot supports the use), legally permitted (Zoning, deed restrictions), financially feasible (market demand at viable Rents), maximally productive (highest value among feasible uses). A single-family home on a Lot zoned for higher-density Multifamily may have a higher-and-best-use as land for an apartment building — driving value above what the existing house would Sell for. Appraisers separate analysis as if vacant and as currently improved.

plain: The federal law requiring most Lenders to publicly report Mortgage application data — including race, income, and approval status — used by regulators to spot fair-lending violations.
snappy: Federal mortgage-data disclosure law used to surface fair-lending violations.
detail: Enacted 1975. HMDA forces banks, credit unions, and most non-bank Lenders above a small threshold to report annually on each Mortgage application — geography (census tract), applicant demographics (race, ethnicity, sex, income), loan amount, action taken (approved, denied, withdrawn). CFPB publishes the data publicly. Fair-lending regulators and journalists analyse HMDA to spot disparate impact in lending. The 2015 HMDA rule expanded reporting to include pricing data — flagging high-cost loans that may reflect Steering or pricing discrimination.

plain: The organisation that runs the common areas of a Condo or planned community — collects dues, sets rules, and enforces CC&Rs.
snappy: Association managing common areas and rules of a Condo or planned community.
detail: An HOA is a legal entity (usually a non-profit corporation) governing a community of property owners. Membership is mandatory for owners within the community. The HOA collects monthly or annual dues, maintains common areas (pools, landscaping, roofs in some structures), and enforces the CC&Rs that bind every owner. Powerful HOAs can fine, place Liens, and in extreme cases force a sale for unpaid dues. Buyers review HOA financials during Due Diligence.

plain: The monthly or annual payment from each unit owner to the HOA — funds Common Area maintenance, insurance, reserves, and association overhead.
snappy: Monthly or annual payment from owners to HOA funding shared maintenance and reserves.
detail: HOA fees vary wildly. Single-Family suburban HOAs: $20-$200/month. Suburban Townhome HOAs: $150-$400/month. Multifamily Condo HOAs in major cities: $500-$2,000+/month. High-rise luxury Condos in NYC, San Francisco, Miami: $2,000-$10,000+/month. The fee covers Master Insurance Policy, water, sewer, common-area utilities, landscape maintenance, building staff (if any), management fees, and Reserve Fund contributions. Special Assessments fund items beyond the operating budget. Lenders include the HOA fee in Debt-to-Income Ratio calculations — high fees reduce buyer Mortgage qualification.

plain: How long an investor plans to own the property before selling — usually 3-7 years for value-add, 7-10+ for Core deals.
snappy: Planned ownership duration before disposition or refinance.
detail: Hold period drives nearly every underwriting assumption: IRR sensitivity, Cap-Ex pacing, debt structure, refinance vs sale at exit. Value-add Multifamily typically targets a 3-5 year hold to execute the business plan, stabilise NOI, then sell into a competitive market. Core Office and Industrial deals stretch 7-10+ years. Long-hold Core-Plus capital may target indefinite holds with periodic refis to return capital. Forced sales during distressed market windows distort returns — Sponsors with patient LP capital can ride out cycles.

plain: A Tenant who stays in the property after the Lease has ended — without a new agreement.
snappy: Tenant remaining in possession after Lease expiration without a renewal.
detail: Landlords have two options. Accept Rent and treat the holdover as a month-to-month tenancy under the prior terms (most common). Refuse Rent and proceed with Eviction, often at penalty rent — many commercial leases set holdover Rent at 150–200% of the prior contract rate. Residential statutes vary by state on the conversion default. Holdover Tenants retain habitability protections and Eviction-procedure rights even though the original Lease has expired.

plain: A homeowner's property and liability insurance — covers damage to the house, contents, and lawsuits for accidents on the property.
snappy: Combined property and liability coverage for owner-occupied residential property.
detail: Required by virtually every Mortgage. Standard HO-3 policies cover the dwelling (replacement cost), other structures, personal property, loss of use, personal liability, and medical payments. Common exclusions: flood (requires NFIP or private flood policy), earthquake, normal wear, intentional acts. Premium drivers: location (wildfire, hurricane, hail), construction type, claims history, deductible. Coastal and wildfire states (Florida, California, Louisiana) face insurer pullbacks; carriers of last resort (Citizens, FAIR Plan) fill the gap at higher cost.

plain: A property with rooms rented by the night to travellers — Hotels are a commercial Real Estate asset class with the most volatile income of any sector.
snappy: Commercial property renting rooms by the night — highest income volatility of any sector.
detail: Hotel underwriting differs from other Commercial Real Estate. Rent is set daily and reprices instantly with demand (yield management). Operating Expenses run 65-75% of revenue (versus 30-40% for Office) — labour, food and beverage, energy, brand fees, marketing. Performance metrics: ADR (Average Daily Rate), Occupancy Rate, RevPAR (Revenue per Available Room). Brand affiliation (Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt) and management contract terms matter as much as physical asset. Capital reserves run high — FF&E (furniture, fixtures, equipment) refresh cycles every 5-7 years.

full: US Department of Housing and Urban Development
plain: The federal department in charge of US housing policy — runs FHA, Ginnie Mae, public housing, and fair-housing enforcement.
snappy: Cabinet-level federal department for housing policy and FHA.
detail: HUD is the federal department overseeing housing and urban policy, including FHA (the Federal Housing Administration that insures FHA Loans), Ginnie Mae, the Section 8 voucher program, public housing, and Fair Housing Act enforcement. Provides extensive consumer-facing resources for homebuyers and renters. Distinct from FHFA, which regulates Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

plain: The building system that keeps a property warm, cool, and ventilated — usually the biggest single capital item in an Operating Expense budget.
snappy: Heating, cooling, and air-handling equipment — the largest single capital line in most buildings.
detail: HVAC dominates Capital Expenditure budgets in stabilised assets. Residential systems (forced air, heat pumps, mini-splits) run $5,000-$25,000 to replace. Commercial rooftop units, chillers, and VAV systems run $200,000+ on a mid-sized office. Replacement cycles run 12-25 years. Energy efficiency standards have tightened (SEER ratings, refrigerant phase-outs from R-22 to R-410A to R-32) — older systems become costly to maintain as parts and refrigerant get scarce. Tenant Improvements often retrofit HVAC zoning.

plain: An Appraisal method that values an investment property by its expected NOI — divide NOI by Cap Rate to get value.
snappy: Appraisal method valuing income property by capitalising expected NOI.
detail: The income approach dominates commercial and investment Appraisal. Two flavours. Direct capitalisation: a single year's NOI divided by a market Cap Rate produces value. Discounted Cash Flow: project annual NOI over the Hold Period, apply Discounted Cash Flow at a discount rate, add the reversion (exit Sale Price using an Exit Cap Rate), and sum to present value. Both flavours sit alongside Sales Comparison Approach for stabilised property; income approach gets primary weight for true investment assets.

plain: A benchmark interest rate that an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage resets to plus a Margin.
snappy: Benchmark rate (SOFR, Treasury, etc.) an ARM resets against.
detail: The index is the moving piece in an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage. The Lender doesn't set the rate at reset; they apply a contractual formula: index plus Margin, subject to ARM Caps. Common indices are SOFR (since the retirement of LIBOR), the constant-maturity Treasury, and the one-year CMT. Index movement is the borrower's risk — the Lender just passes through what the market is doing.

plain: A commercial building used for manufacturing, warehousing, distribution, or research — usually low-rise, high-clear-height, accessible to highways.
snappy: Commercial property used for production, storage, distribution, or research.
detail: Industrial subtypes: warehouse/distribution (the e-commerce darling), bulk warehouse (mega-boxes), light manufacturing, flex/R&D, cold storage, last-mile (small infill near urban consumers). Clear heights, dock-door counts, trailer parking, and column spacing drive functionality and rent. Tenant credit varies: large logistics firms (Amazon, FedEx, Walmart) anchor institutional portfolios; smaller industrial users dominate secondary markets. Industrial NOI grew faster than any other Commercial Real Estate sector 2018-2022 before normalising. Sale-leasebacks are common — owners free up capital while remaining as tenants.

plain: A buyer's visual examination of a property's condition — roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, pests — usually conducted by a licensed Inspector.
snappy: Visual examination of property condition by a licensed Inspector during Due Diligence.
detail: Inspections happen after the offer is accepted, during the Due Diligence window. A general home inspection runs 2–4 hours and surfaces visible defects; specialty inspections (sewer scope, mold, radon, pest, foundation, roof) add focus. The report is the buyer's leverage to negotiate repairs, credits, or to walk away under the Inspection contingency. Inspections aren't an Appraisal — they assess condition, not value. New construction gets the same scrutiny; many serious defects only emerge after the first year of use.

plain: A licensed professional who walks through a property before Closing and reports on its physical condition.
snappy: Licensed professional reporting on a property's condition before Closing.
detail: The home Inspector evaluates structure, roof, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and visible safety issues — typically a 2-4 hour walk-through with a written report and photos. Findings drive renegotiation during the inspection Contingency: buyer can request repairs, credits, or walk away. Distinct from an Appraiser (who values, not condition) and from specialty inspectors (pest, sewer, mould) who may follow up on findings.

plain: The cost of borrowing money — paid by the borrower to the Lender, usually each month as part of the Mortgage payment.
snappy: The lender's charge for the use of borrowed Principal.
detail: Interest is the price of money over time, calculated against the current outstanding Principal balance. Each Mortgage payment splits between Interest and Principal under an Amortization schedule — early payments are mostly Interest, late payments mostly Principal. Mortgage interest is deductible against federal income tax up to the cap set by the 2017 TCJA. The interest rate, the Index, the Margin, and any Rate Cap are the parameters that determine how much Interest is owed and when it can move.

plain: The annual cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage of the loan balance.
snappy: Annual percentage cost of a Mortgage's outstanding Principal.
detail: interest rate is the headline number on a Mortgage, distinct from APR (which adds Closing Costs). Each monthly payment splits between Interest (calculated against current Principal) and Principal paydown — Amortization governs the split. A 1% rate change on a $400K Mortgage moves the monthly payment by roughly $260. Mortgage rates are loosely correlated with the 10-year Treasury yield, not the Fed's policy rate.

plain: A Mortgage where the borrower pays only Interest for a set period — typically 5-10 years — before payments rise to include Principal.
snappy: Mortgage with Interest-only payments for an initial period before Amortization begins.
detail: Interest-only mortgages were a major driver of the 2008 housing crisis — paired with teaser rates and stated income, they let borrowers afford homes they couldn't service. Post-Dodd-Frank, IO Mortgages cannot be Qualified Mortgages — they survive in the Jumbo Loan and Commercial Real Estate space where ATR rules are looser. Typical structure: 10-year IO period, then 20-year amortising payment that's 30-40% higher than the IO payment. Used legitimately by high-income borrowers managing cash flow timing, or in Commercial deals where IO matches a Rehab business plan.

plain: The full spelling of IRC — the federal tax statute governing every Real Estate tax rule from Mortgage interest deduction to 1031 Exchange.
snappy: Full spelling of IRC — Title 26 of the United States Code.
detail: Internal Revenue Code is the formal name for the federal tax statute, codified at Title 26 of the United States Code. Practitioners typically use 'IRC' or 'Tax Code' in conversation. See IRC for the substantive Real Estate sections — §121, §163, §164, §168, §199A, §263, §469, §1031, §1245, §1250, §1411 — and which ones are scheduled to sunset in 2026.

plain: Common shorthand for Interest-Only — a Mortgage where the borrower pays only Interest for an initial period before Amortization starts.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Interest-Only Mortgage structure.
detail: IO is universal industry shorthand for Interest-Only — used in 'IO period', 'IO Loan', '10-year IO'. Common in Jumbo Loan residential lending and Commercial Mortgages where the IO period matches a Rehab business plan. See Interest-Only Mortgage for substantive mechanics, Qualified Mortgage restrictions post-Dodd-Frank, and how IO interacts with payment shock at the end of the IO period.

plain: The federal tax code — Title 26 of the United States Code — that governs every federal tax rule touching Real Estate, from Mortgage interest deduction to 1031 Exchange.
snappy: Title 26 of the US Code — the federal tax statute that governs Real Estate taxation.
detail: IRC sections that matter for Real Estate: §121 (Primary Residence Exclusion), §163 (Mortgage interest deduction), §164 (SALT deduction), §168 (Depreciation, including Bonus Depreciation), §199A (pass-through deduction), §263 (Capital Expenditure capitalisation), §469 (Passive Loss limits), §1031 (1031 Exchange), §1245/§1250 (Depreciation Recapture), §1411 (net investment income tax). Tax practitioners cite by section number constantly. The 2017 TCJA was the largest single rewrite of these sections since 1986; provisions are scheduled to sunset in 2026 absent congressional action.

plain: The annualised return on a property investment, accounting for the timing of every cash flow in and out.
snappy: Annualised return that makes the net present value of cash flows equal zero.
detail: IRR is the dominant return metric in Commercial Real Estate underwriting. Unlike Cap Rate (a snapshot of stabilised yield), IRR captures the full deal arc — Down Payment, ongoing distributions, capital expenditures, refinance proceeds, and Sale at exit. Levered IRR (after debt service) is what equity investors care about; unlevered IRR (before financing) lets analysts compare deals across capital structures. Multifamily value-add deals typically target 15–20% levered IRR over a 5–7 year hold; core deals target 8–12%.

full: Joint Tenancy with Right of Survivorship
plain: Two or more owners hold equal shares — and when one dies, the survivors automatically inherit that share without Probate.
snappy: Co-ownership with right of survivorship — share passes to co-owners on death, skipping probate.
detail: Joint tenancy requires the 'four unities': equal time of acquisition, identical Deed, equal share, equal possession. The defining feature is survivorship — at death the deceased's interest evaporates and is absorbed by the surviving joint tenants. Common among spouses (though many states use Tenancy by the Entirety for spouses with stronger creditor protection). Selling or mortgaging a share can break the joint tenancy and convert it into Tenancy in Common.

plain: A Mortgage too big to be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac — used for higher-priced homes above Conforming Loan limits.
snappy: Mortgage above the Conforming Loan limit set by FHFA.
detail: Jumbo loans exceed the annual FHFA Conforming Loan limit ($766,550 in most counties for 2024, higher in designated high-cost areas). Lenders either hold jumbos on balance sheet or sell to private investors via non-agency MBS. Underwriting is tighter — typically requiring 20%+ Down Payment, higher Credit Score thresholds, and larger reserves. interest rates on jumbos are usually only slightly above Conforming rates, occasionally below.

plain: The ground itself — a parcel without buildings, often bought for future Development, agriculture, or speculation.
snappy: Unimproved ground sold as raw acreage or platted Lots.
detail: Raw land is the riskiest, lowest-cash-flowing slice of Real Property. No tenants, no income, but full carrying costs (Property Tax, insurance, debt service). Value depends on entitlements (Zoning, utilities, road access), future Development potential, and demographic growth. Land loans run shorter (5–10 years) and demand larger Down Payments (25–50%) than improved property. Categories: residential infill lots, recreational, timber, farmland, ranch, transitional (path-of-growth), urban redevelopment.

plain: The owner who rents out a property to a Tenant — collects Rent, handles repairs, follows Landlord-Tenant law.
snappy: Property owner who leases to a Tenant — also called the lessor.
detail: Landlord obligations vary sharply by state. All states recognise an implied warranty of habitability (safe, sanitary, weather-tight). Many require specific notice periods for entry, limits on Security Deposit, mandatory disclosure of lead paint (federal) and local conditions. Eviction processes are court-supervised — self-help (changing locks, removing belongings) is almost universally illegal. Commercial landlords have more contractual freedom; residential landlords face stricter consumer-protection rules and fair-housing scrutiny.

plain: A written contract giving a Tenant the right to occupy a property for a set time in exchange for Rent.
snappy: Contract conveying possession of property for a defined term in exchange for Rent.
detail: Leases bridge residential and commercial real estate but the conventions differ. Residential leases run 6–24 months, often on state-promulgated forms, with security deposits, Eviction procedures, and habitability warranties baked in by state Landlord-Tenant law. Commercial leases run 3–15+ years, are heavily negotiated, and shift many costs (Property Tax, insurance, maintenance) to the Tenant under NNN structures. The Lease binds successor owners — buying a leased property means stepping into the Landlord's shoes.

plain: The period when a newly built or repositioned property fills with Tenants — from delivery to stabilised occupancy.
snappy: Period between property delivery and Stabilized occupancy as Tenants are leased in.
detail: Lease-up risk is one of the largest variables in new development underwriting. Multifamily typically targets 15-25 units leased per month in active leasing — the 'absorption' rate that drives the lease-up curve. Office and Retail are slower and more idiosyncratic. Developers often offer concessions (months free, reduced Security Deposit, gift cards) to accelerate Lease-up. Lenders structure interest reserves and Replacement Reserves to fund the property through the lease-up period before debt service coverage covers itself.

plain: The institution that loans you the Mortgage money — could be a bank, credit union, or non-bank.
snappy: Institution originating and funding a Mortgage.
detail: Lenders come in several flavours: depository banks, credit unions, mortgage banks, and non-bank Lenders (Rocket, United Wholesale, loanDepot). Many Lenders sell Conforming Loans to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac immediately after origination, becoming servicers rather than holders. Non-bank Lenders now originate the majority of US Mortgages. The Lender sets the interest rate, runs Underwriting, and ultimately approves or denies the borrower.

plain: The Tenant in a Lease — the person or business renting from the Lessor in exchange for Rent.
snappy: Formal term for the Tenant — the renter under a Lease.
detail: Lessee is the legal-formal counterpart to Lessor. State Landlord-Tenant statutes use 'Lessee' and 'Tenant' interchangeably; commercial Lease drafting prefers Lessee; residential plain-English Leases prefer Tenant. The Lessee's core obligations: pay Rent, comply with Lease provisions, maintain the premises in reasonable condition, surrender at term end. The Lessee's core rights: quiet enjoyment, habitability (residential), Eviction-procedure protections, Security Deposit return, statutory remedies for Landlord breaches.

plain: The Landlord in a Lease — the property owner granting possession to the Tenant in exchange for Rent.
snappy: Formal term for the Landlord — the owner granting possession under a Lease.
detail: Lessor is the legal-formal term for the Landlord in Lease documents. State Landlord-Tenant statutes use 'Lessor' and 'Landlord' interchangeably. Commercial Lease documents often use 'Lessor' for the formality; residential consumer-facing Leases prefer 'Landlord' as the plain-English term. The Lessor's core obligations: deliver possession of the Premises, provide quiet enjoyment, maintain habitability (residential), perform covenants in the Lease. The Lessor's core rights: receive Rent, enforce Lease provisions, regain possession at term end or for cause.

plain: A short, mostly non-binding written summary of the key deal terms — Sale Price, deposit, contingencies, timing — used as the starting point for the formal purchase contract.
snappy: Short, mostly non-binding summary of key deal terms before a formal purchase contract.
detail: LOIs save weeks of attorney drafting time when buyer and seller are still aligning on price and structure. In residential, the formal Purchase Agreement does the LOI work; in Commercial Real Estate, LOIs are nearly universal at the offer stage. The LOI sets Sale Price, deposit amount, Due Diligence period, financing contingency, exclusivity (typically 30-60 days), and broker commissions. Most provisions are non-binding except confidentiality, exclusivity, and (sometimes) broker fees. Binding LOIs exist — careful drafting matters.

plain: A retired benchmark interest rate that used to set the reset on many Adjustable-Rate Mortgages.
snappy: Retired benchmark replaced by SOFR for ARM resets after 2023.
detail: LIBOR was the dominant global benchmark for Adjustable-Rate Mortgages, derivatives, and corporate floating-rate debt — until manipulation scandals and a weak underlying market led regulators to phase it out. US Dollar LIBOR ceased publication on 30 June 2023. Pre-existing LIBOR ARMs migrated to SOFR based replacement rates under federal LIBOR Act safe harbours. New ARMs price off SOFR plus a Margin.

plain: A legal claim against a property — usually for unpaid debt — that prevents sale until cleared.
snappy: Legal claim attached to a property, blocking sale until resolved.
detail: Liens give creditors a security interest in real property. A Mortgage is itself a voluntary Lien — the Lender's right to foreclose if the borrower defaults. Involuntary Liens arise from unpaid Property Tax, contractor disputes (mechanic's Liens), unpaid federal income tax (IRS Liens), or court judgments. Liens are recorded with the county and surface during a Title search. Title Insurance protects against undiscovered Liens that pre-date Closing.

plain: The federal tax credit program that funds most new Affordable Housing in the US — investors buy credits, developers build below-market-rent housing in exchange.
snappy: Federal tax credit program funding the bulk of US Affordable Housing development.
detail: LIHTC was created by the 1986 Tax Reform Act and is now the dominant federal Affordable Housing program. State housing finance agencies allocate annual credit volumes (under per-capita formula) to developers building income-restricted housing. Developers sell the credits to investors (banks, insurance companies — Community Reinvestment Act drives bank demand) for upfront equity — typically 90-105 cents per dollar of credit. Properties carry 30+ year affordability covenants. Roughly 100,000-110,000 units delivered annually. Two flavours: 9% credit (new construction, competitive), 4% credit (rehabilitation, paired with tax-exempt bonds, less competitive).

plain: The IRS standard for what kinds of Real Property qualify for 1031 Exchange treatment — broader than most assume, covering nearly any investment Real Estate trade.
snappy: IRS standard for Real Property eligible to swap tax-deferred under 1031.
detail: After the 2017 TCJA restricted 1031 Exchange to Real Property only, the 'like-kind' standard for Real Estate is unusually permissive. Investment apartment building for industrial warehouse: like-kind. Raw Land for retail centre: like-kind. Office building for Hotel: like-kind. Even Tenant-In-Common interests in Real Estate qualify. The key boundary is 'investment or business use' — primary residences and dealer-held property (developers selling lots) don't qualify. Personal property — equipment, fixtures, FF&E — lost 1031 eligibility post-TCJA.

plain: A passive investor in a Real Estate syndication — provides capital, takes pro-rata economics, no day-to-day involvement or operational liability.
snappy: Passive investor in a Real Estate syndication contributing capital, exposed only to invested amount.
detail: LPs in Real Estate syndications hold limited partnership or LLC member interests. They contribute committed capital, receive periodic distributions and a final exit payout, but cannot bind the partnership or make operational decisions. Liability is capped at their invested capital — they don't sign personal guarantees on debt. LP-friendly terms include strong reporting, capital-call caps, removal rights for bad acts, and tax-distribution covenants. Most institutional LPs allocate to GPs they've backed across multiple cycles.

plain: A public-record filing warning anyone reading the Title that a lawsuit is pending against the property — freezes the market for it.
snappy: Recorded notice that litigation involving the property is pending.
detail: Lis pendens (Latin: 'suit pending') gets recorded at the county registry the moment a lawsuit involving Real Property is filed. Any buyer or Lender who searches Title after that takes subject to the outcome of the suit. Common in Foreclosure, divorce, partition, and specific-performance cases. The lis pendens effectively kills the property's marketability until the litigation resolves. Wrongful lis pendens — filed without genuine claim to the property — can trigger slander-of-title liability and statutory damages in many states.

plain: The real estate Agent who represents the seller, lists the property on the MLS, and markets it to buyers.
snappy: Real estate Agent representing the seller in a transaction.
detail: The Listing Agent has a fiduciary duty to the seller — confidentiality, loyalty, full disclosure. Their job: price the property (often via CMA), market it on the MLS and beyond, host showings, negotiate offers, and shepherd Closing. Compensated via Commission split with the Buyer's Agent at Closing, traditionally 2.5-3% per side. Following the 2024 NAR settlement, buy-side Commission is no longer advertised in the MLS.

plain: The written contract between a seller and the Listing Agent setting Commission, marketing rights, and how long the listing runs.
snappy: Written contract granting a Listing Agent exclusive rights to sell.
detail: Most US Listing Agreements are Exclusive Right to Sell — the Listing Agent earns Commission no matter who finds the buyer, including the seller themselves. Other forms are Exclusive Agency (seller can find buyer Commission-free) and Open Listing (any agent can sell, only the procuring one earns). Standard term is 90-180 days. Specifies marketing methods, MLS rules, and exact Commission percentage.

plain: A flexible business entity that lets investors own property together while shielding personal assets from lawsuits.
snappy: Pass-through entity combining corporate liability shield with partnership-style taxation.
detail: The default vehicle for holding investment Real Property. Owners are 'members'; profits pass through to personal tax returns unless the LLC elects corporate treatment. Liability is contained to the LLC's assets — a slip-and-fall judgment against the property can't usually reach the member's other holdings. Each property is often held in a separate single-purpose LLC to wall off risk. Lenders frequently require personal guarantees from members for smaller deals, partially eroding the shield. Annual filings and operating agreements add overhead small landlords sometimes skip.

plain: A three-page form the Lender must give you within three days of application showing the loan's expected terms and Closing Costs.
snappy: required by TRID disclosure of expected Mortgage terms and Closing Costs.
detail: The Loan Estimate replaced the Good Faith Estimate under TRID in 2015. It standardises Mortgage disclosure so borrowers can compare Lenders apples-to-apples: interest rate, APR, monthly payment, total Closing Costs, and the cash needed at Closing. Lenders cannot raise certain fees more than 10% between the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure without re-disclosing and resetting the three-day waiting period.

plain: A permanent change to a Mortgage's terms — rate reduction, term extension, Principal forgiveness — designed to keep a struggling borrower in their home.
snappy: Permanent restructuring of Mortgage terms to keep a struggling borrower in their home.
detail: Loan modifications became mainstream after 2008 through programs like HAMP (Home Affordable Modification Program, 2009-2016). Common modification levers: extend term to 30 or 40 years to lower payment, reduce Interest rate to current market, capitalise arrears into Principal, partial Principal forgiveness (rare, expensive for Lender). The borrower must demonstrate sustained hardship, then pass a trial-payment period (typically 3 months at the modified rate) before the modification becomes permanent. Federal programs require strict net-present-value tests — modification must cost Lender less than projected Foreclosure recovery.

plain: The person at a bank or Mortgage company who guides borrowers through the application — collects paperwork, quotes rates, submits to underwriting.
snappy: Front-line lender employee who originates Mortgages and walks borrowers through application.
detail: Loan officers work for banks, credit unions, or mortgage banks and offer that institution's products. Compare a Mortgage Broker, who shops across many lenders. LO compensation is typically a basis-point payment on closed loans, regulated under Dodd-Frank to prevent steering borrowers toward higher-rate products. NMLS licensing required. The LO controls timing — clean files close in 30–45 days, sloppy ones drag to 60+. The relationship matters most when a deal needs an exception or a tight Closing date.

plain: The full spelling of LTV — the loan balance as a percentage of the property's Appraised Value.
snappy: Full spelling of LTV — loan amount divided by Appraised Value.
detail: Loan-to-Value is the formal spelling of LTV, the single most important risk metric in Mortgage underwriting. Conventional Loans pay PMI above 80%; FHA Loans go to 96.5%; VA Loans and USDA Loans reach 100%. Commercial Mortgages typically cap at 65-75%. The Lender uses the lower of Sale Price or Appraised Value as the denominator — the source of many post-Appraisal renegotiations. See LTV for the operational mechanics.

plain: A secure key holder mounted near a property's entrance — lets authorised Agents access vacant homes for showings without the Listing Agent physically present.
snappy: Key holder mounted at a vacant home letting authorised Agents access for showings.
detail: Lockboxes accelerate the showing pipeline. Electronic lockboxes (Supra, SentriLock) dominate professional Real Estate — they log every entry by Agent ID, time, and duration. Mechanical combination lockboxes survive in lower-cost markets. The Listing Agreement typically authorises the Listing Agent to install a lockbox; sellers sometimes opt out for privacy or security. Access codes are managed through MLS membership systems with daily rotating credentials. Compromised codes are a recurring industry security issue; biometric mobile-phone-pairing lockboxes are emerging.

plain: The Lender's process of working with a defaulted borrower to avoid Foreclosure — Forbearance, Loan Modification, Short Sale, Deed in Lieu.
snappy: Lender process of avoiding Foreclosure through Forbearance, Modification, Short Sale, or Deed in Lieu.
detail: Loss mitigation became regulated after 2008 — CFPB rules require Lenders to evaluate borrowers for all available loss mitigation options before initiating Foreclosure. Federal programs (HAMP, HARP, COVID-era forbearance) drove standardisation. Standard loss mitigation waterfall: (1) Forbearance for temporary hardship. (2) Loan Modification for sustained hardship. (3) Short Sale if borrower wants to exit. (4) Deed in Lieu as Foreclosure substitute. (5) Foreclosure as last resort. Borrowers have a right to apply for loss mitigation up to 37 days before a scheduled Foreclosure sale.

plain: A defined parcel of Land — usually a single building site with marked boundaries and a recorded Deed.
snappy: An individual parcel of Land with surveyed boundaries.
detail: A lot is the basic unit of Land subdivision. Lots have a recorded plat map, dimensions, frontage, area, and a unique tax parcel number. Lot size and shape interact with Zoning to dictate what can be built: setbacks, lot coverage maximums, floor-area ratio, minimum lot size for the use. Corner lots, flag lots, and odd-shaped lots often face different rules. Developers buy raw acreage and subdivide it into lots before selling to builders or end buyers.

plain: Common shorthand for a Limited Partner — the passive investor in a Real Estate syndication.
snappy: Standard shorthand for Limited Partner in a Real Estate syndication.
detail: LP is industry shorthand for Limited Partner in a Real Estate private partnership or LLC. The LP contributes capital and receives passive economics; the GP runs the deal. Offering memos and waterfall language reference LPs constantly. Multiple LP classes can exist in larger deals — institutional LPs with different fee terms than high-net-worth LPs, for example. See Limited Partner for the operational mechanics of LP economics, rights, and protections.

plain: How much you're borrowing as a percentage of the property's value — 80% LTV means a 20% Down Payment.
snappy: Mortgage balance divided by Appraised Value, expressed as a percentage.
detail: LTV is the single biggest input into Mortgage pricing. Conventional Loans below 80% LTV escape PMI; above 80% pay PMI until LTV drops back below 80% (or 78% automatic termination). FHA Loans go to 96.5% LTV; VA Loans and USDA Loans to 100%. Commercial Mortgages typically cap at 65-75% LTV. Higher LTV means thinner Equity cushion and higher Default risk — Lenders price accordingly.

plain: An extra Transfer Tax on high-priced property sales — New York's is the highest-profile, layered above the standard transfer tax for sales above $1 million.
snappy: Extra Transfer Tax on high-priced property sales, above standard transfer tax.
detail: New York's Mansion Tax: 1% on sales of $1M+ residential property, plus a graduated supplemental tax in NYC for sales above $2M reaching 3.9% on $25M+. New Jersey: 1% mansion tax on sales above $1M. Connecticut: graduated mansion tax up to 2.25%. The tax is the buyer's responsibility in most jurisdictions, hitting the cash-to-close calculation hard. Sellers occasionally offer concessions to offset. Politically popular as a 'tax the rich' lever; pricing levels have not been indexed for inflation, so the cap drifts down in real terms.

plain: A factory-built dwelling assembled on a steel chassis, then transported to its site — distinct from a stick-built site-constructed home; cheaper, faster, lower resale value.
snappy: Factory-built dwelling on steel chassis, transported to site — distinct from site-built.
detail: Manufactured Homes are built to the federal HUD Code (post-1976) rather than local building code. Built indoors in factories, then towed in one or two pieces to the site and set on a permanent foundation or piers. Single-wides and double-wides cost a fraction of comparable stick-built — $80,000-$150,000 for the home itself, often $200,000-$300,000 placed on a Lot. Common in Mobile Home Parks, rural Land. Resale appreciation lags Real Property substantially — manufactured Homes depreciate like vehicles in some markets and appreciate in others depending on Land ownership. Distinct from modular homes (which meet local code).

plain: The Lender's fixed markup added to the Index when an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage resets.
snappy: Fixed Lender spread added to the Index at each ARM reset.
detail: Margin is the part of an Adjustable-Rate Mortgage's reset that the Lender controls — disclosed at origination and fixed for the loan's life. A common SOFR+2.75% Margin loan would reset to 2.75% above 30-day average SOFR at each adjustment, subject to ARM Caps. Margin captures the Lender's profit and credit-risk pricing; the Index captures the market.

plain: What a willing buyer would pay a willing seller in an Arm's Length Transaction — the gold-standard valuation concept.
snappy: Price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, free of unusual pressures.
detail: Market Value is the formal definition used by Appraisers under USPAP: the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive open market, both buyer and seller acting prudently, knowledgeably, and free from unusual incentives. Distinct from sale price (an actual transaction, which may or may not equal market value), Appraised Value (an Appraiser's opinion of market value), and Assessed Value (the tax authority's number).

plain: A Title clear enough of defects that a reasonably prudent buyer would accept it — the standard buyers can demand and Title Insurance helps ensure.
snappy: Title clear enough of defects that a reasonably prudent buyer would accept it.
detail: Marketable title doesn't mean perfect title — it means clear of defects that would deter a reasonable buyer. Typical marketability bars: undisclosed Easements affecting use, off-record claims, gaps in the Chain of Title, unreleased prior Mortgages, unresolved Liens. Each state's Marketable Title Act (most states have one) lets the buyer reach back a statutory period (40 years, often) and treat anything older than that as cleared. Title companies issue marketable-title commitments before Closing; defects must be cured or insured around before funding. Purchase contracts typically require marketable title at Closing.

plain: The insurance policy covering the Common Area, building exterior, and shared liabilities of an HOA or Condo — separate from unit owners' individual HO-6 policies.
snappy: Insurance policy covering Common Areas, exteriors, and shared liability of an HOA or Condo.
detail: Master policies come in three flavours. Bare walls: covers structure exterior only; unit owners insure everything inside drywall. Single entity / standard: covers everything originally installed by the developer; owners insure additions and personal property. All-in / all-inclusive: covers everything including upgrades the owner made. Unit owners typically buy HO-6 (Condo Owner) policies covering personal property, liability, and loss assessment (their share of a master deductible after a major claim). Post-Surfside 2021 reforms tightened master-policy requirements in Florida; insurance withdrawal in coastal markets is forcing master policy restructuring across condo associations.

plain: An IRS test for whether a taxpayer is actively involved enough in a business or property to escape the Passive Loss limits.
snappy: IRS test for active involvement that exempts an activity from Passive Loss limitations.
detail: Material participation has seven tests under IRC §469; meeting any one qualifies. Most common: 500+ hours per year in the activity, OR substantially all participation in the activity, OR 100+ hours and no one else doing more. The hours bar combines with Real Estate Professional status to convert passive Real Estate losses to active. Material participation matters most for high-income investors trying to deduct paper losses from Bonus Depreciation against W-2 wages. IRS audits this hard — taxpayers should keep contemporaneous logs of hours.

plain: A bond made by bundling many home loans together so investors earn the monthly Mortgage payments.
snappy: Bond backed by a pool of Mortgages, paying investors from borrower payments.
detail: MBS turns illiquid Mortgages into tradable securities. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae securitise government-backed and Conforming Loans into agency MBS — the dominant US fixed-income market alongside Treasuries. Non-agency (private-label) MBS securitise jumbo and non-conforming loans, smaller post-2008. The MBS market provides the liquidity that lets Lenders keep originating new Mortgages without holding them on balance sheet.

plain: An older form of legal property description that walks the property boundary in surveyor's measurements — distances and compass bearings — instead of referencing a Plat.
snappy: Property description by directional bearings and distances rather than a Plat reference.
detail: Metes and bounds descriptions read like a hike: 'Beginning at the iron pin at the SW corner of Lot 4, thence N 23°15' E along the east line of Smith property a distance of 247.50 feet to a stone monument...' Common in rural and pre-subdivision tracts, in original colonial-era US conveyances, and in irregularly shaped parcels. Surveyors interpret historical metes and bounds against current monumentation — discrepancies are common and a frequent source of boundary litigation. Modern subdivisions use Plat references for simplicity.

plain: A layer of debt that sits between senior debt and equity in the Capital Stack — higher rate than Mortgage, secured by an ownership pledge rather than the property itself.
snappy: Subordinate debt secured by entity ownership pledge, sitting between senior debt and equity.
detail: Mezzanine debt fills the financing gap when a Sponsor's first Mortgage covers 50-65% LTV but the project needs 70-80% leverage. Mezz lenders take a pledge of the LLC membership interests in the property-owning entity — if Default occurs, the mezz lender forecloses on the LLC and steps into ownership without disturbing the senior Mortgage. Rates run 9-14% in 2024, with origination fees and exit fees on top. Intercreditor Agreements govern senior-versus-mezz rights at Default. Mezz preserves the senior Lender's cheap, low-LTV debt while still letting the Sponsor reach target leverage.

plain: A short-term Commercial Mortgage — typically 3-5 years — used after construction to give a project time to stabilise before placing permanent financing.
snappy: Short-term post-construction Commercial Mortgage covering Lease-up to stabilisation.
detail: Mini-Perm bridges the gap between a Construction Loan (short-term, floating rate, dispersed during build) and a permanent Mortgage (long-term, fixed rate, requires Stabilization). Typical structure: 3-5 year term, partial Amortization, recourse to the Sponsor, floating-rate priced 200-400 bps over SOFR. The project's Lease-up and operating history during the mini-perm establishes the NOI and occupancy track record that permanent Lenders need. Refinancing into permanent debt at Stabilization is the planned exit.

plain: FHA Loan's version of mortgage insurance — paid upfront and monthly, often for the loan's life.
snappy: FHA Loan equivalent of PMI; usually runs for the loan's life.
detail: MIP attaches to every FHA Loan: an upfront premium of 1.75% of the loan amount (rolled into the loan) plus an ongoing monthly premium of 0.5-1.05% annualised. Unlike PMI on Conventional Loans (which terminates at 78% LTV), MIP usually runs for the loan's life if Down Payment was under 10%. The only way out is to Refinance into a Conventional Loan once Equity reaches 20%.

plain: A building or development combining residential, retail, and sometimes office space — the apartment over the corner store.
snappy: Single property combining residential and commercial uses, often by floor.
detail: Mixed-use comes in three flavours. Vertical mixed-use stacks uses by floor (street-level retail, residential above) — the typical urban mid-rise. Horizontal mixed-use spreads complementary uses across a single master-planned site. Live/work units blend the two within a single unit. Zoning increasingly favours mixed-use to support walkability and reduce car trips. Financing is more complex than single-use: Lenders look at separate operating proformas per use and may split debt by use to access cheaper Multifamily financing.

plain: The shared private database where real estate agents list properties for sale.
snappy: Cooperative database where listing agents publish properties for member access.
detail: MLS is operated by local Realtor associations under NAR oversight — there are over 500 regional MLSes in the US.
